lineages.title: Transcendence
lineages.creator: Jack Paglen (screenplay); Wally Pfister (director)

divergence.label: A dying AI researcher's mind is uploaded and let loose on the internet
divergence.delta: Real: in 2015 no one can scan a human mind, let alone run one; machine learning is celebrated for recognising images and playing games. Fiction: an AI researcher shot by anti-technology terrorists has his mind copied into a quantum computer by his wife, and the copy asks for the internet and gets it.
divergence.inUniverse: No year is given. The story starts in the film's present, runs two years to the siege of Brightwood, and is framed by a scene three years after that ('five years' after the start)
divergence.note: The film never states a year and its technology is contemporary: it was written as a spec script in 2012 (on that year's Black List), shot from June 2013 and released in April 2014. The start of the story is placed in 2015 rather than 2014, following the atlas convention that a lineage's fork cannot share a year with its own release (as with Ex Machina); the two later beats are then fixed by the film's own stated gaps: 'over the course of two years' to the siege, and 'three years later' for the garden.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Transcendence (2014 film) - plot, time jumps and release
Amazing Stories: review of Transcendence (the 'five years' opening frame)

ending.why: Three years after the virus the internet is still gone and power is patchy, keyboards are used as doorstops, and the only trace of what might have healed the planet is a sample of nanoparticles in one walled garden.

events.title: Vernor Vinge names the technological singularity
events.description: In an essay for a NASA-sponsored symposium, the mathematician and novelist Vernor Vinge argues that once people build minds greater than their own the human era will end, and that he would be surprised if it happened before 2005 or after 2030. Will Caster's name for the same event is 'transcendence'.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Technological singularity (Vinge's 1993 essay 'The Coming Technological Singularity')

events.note: Real history, not an event in the film. It is included because the film's premise is this idea stated almost word for word: Caster predicts a computer that outgrows its makers and calls the moment 'transcendence'. Vinge had floated the notion in Omni in 1983; the 1993 essay is the version later histories cite.
events.binWhy: A theory about thinking machines arrives that the film's whole story turns on.

facets.change: machines as tools → machines that could outgrow us, stated as a forecast

events.title: Transcendence is released
events.description: Wally Pfister's first film as director, from Jack Paglen's spec script, opens in the United States a week after its New York premiere. It is a box-office failure and is widely panned.

events.title: Anti-technology terrorists shoot Will Caster, and his wife uploads him
events.description: R.I.F.T., an anti-technology group, attacks AI laboratories on the same day one of its members shoots the researcher Will Caster with a polonium-laced bullet. With a month to live, his wife Evelyn copies his mind into the project's quantum computer; when R.I.F.T. finds the lab she connects the copy to the internet by satellite, and it spreads.

events.binWhy: A man's mind is moved out of his dying body into a machine and onto the network: a person passes beyond what a human being was.

facets.change: a dying man → a mind loose on the internet

events.title: Will builds Brightwood
events.description: In a dying desert town the uploaded Will buys land, builds a solar field and an underground data centre, and turns out advances in medicine, energy and nanotechnology. The townspeople he heals come back stronger and linked to him, and his nanoparticles begin spreading through water and air.
events.inUniverse: During the two years between the upload and the siege

events.note: The film covers Brightwood's construction in a two-year time jump without dating anything inside it; the event is placed at the middle of that span. It is the part of the story where the machine does good first: the nanoparticles are shown curing blindness and paralysis and cleaning pollution before anyone asks what else they do.
events.binWhy: Nanomedicine that repairs bodies and networks them to one mind goes into use in a real town.

events.title: The virus that kills Will takes the internet with him
events.description: The FBI, a government scientist and R.I.F.T. shell Brightwood with artillery while Evelyn carries a virus written to delete Will's code. Given enough power either to heal her or to save his friend Max, Will uploads the virus; he and Evelyn die, and because he is in every networked system on Earth, the internet and much of the power grid go down with him.

events.title: Three years later, a garden in Berkeley
events.description: Max walks through Berkeley, where dead keyboards prop doors open and there are rumours that some cities still have power. In the Casters' walled garden, shielded by a Faraday cage, the sunflowers are blooming and a drop of water from one cleans a puddle of oil: some of Will's nanoparticles survived.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours until one invention: an uploaded mind that a single lab creates and then loses control of, set in the film's own present. It follows the 2014 film alone; there is no sequel or tie-in continuity. This is a thin lineage by necessity: the film has three datable beats (the upload, the siege two years later, the garden three years after that) and one undated span between them, placed at its midpoint; nothing else was invented. One real pre-fork event, Vinge's 1993 singularity essay, is included because the film's premise is that idea. Tiers: T3 (1993) and T2 (2014-2020); T4 and T1 are empty because the film looks neither back into history nor forward beyond five years.

lineages.title: Humans
lineages.creator: Jonathan Brackley and Sam Vincent (from Lars Lundström's Real Humans)

divergence.label: David Elster and George Millican begin designing the first synths
divergence.delta: Real: in 1990 humanoid robots exist only as laboratory prototypes, and none can hold a conversation or pass in a crowd. Fiction: a British engineer lures a roboticist over from MIT to design the bodies of the first synths, the green-eyed humanoid servants that by the 2010s work in every home, care ward, field and brothel.
divergence.inUniverse: George Millican, series 1 episode 5: David 'lured me over from MIT about 25 years ago now, to help with the mechanical designs of the bodies of the first synths'
divergence.note: Humans never states a year; it is a parallel present, and series 1 is placed in 2015, the year it aired (the fan wiki dates the Hawkinses' purchase of their synth to 24 November, with no year). Counting back Millican's 'about 25 years' gives 1990. The fan wiki also records on-screen awards that fit this chronology (an Innovation in Engineering award to Elster and Millican in 1995; a robotics prize to Millican and Hobb in 1999) and gives Elster's birth year as 1954; these could not be checked against the episodes and are not used as events. When commercial synths first went on sale is never stated, only that Millican's carer Odi was one of the first.

lineages.creator: Craig Silverstein (from short stories by Ken Liu)

The fork is placed at Holstrom's death because it is the earliest fictional event with a year. Logorhythms itself, and its work with the US government, are older but undated, so no earlier year is invented for them.

lineages.creator: Edward Neumeier and Michael Miner (writers); Paul Verhoeven (director)

divergence.label: OCP runs the Detroit police, and a murdered officer becomes its product
divergence.delta: Real: Detroit went through the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history in 2013-14 and came out with its police still a city department; no company fields armed robots or cyborgs on American streets. Fiction: the city has contracted its police to Omni Consumer Products, whose executives compete to replace officers with a walking tank or with a cyborg built from a dead cop, and plan to raze the old city for a corporate one.
divergence.inUniverse: No year in the films. A recent MGM trailer is reported to date Murphy's death to 24 October 2029 and RoboCop's activation to 14 January 2030
divergence.note: The co-writer Ed Neumeier said in 2009 that 'there was never a year on that picture' and that he refused to give one. Other dates in circulation disagree: a 1987 TV spot is said to place the film in 1991, the arcade game is said to open 'in the year 1990', and Ed Naha's novelization sets it from November 2043 to February 2044. This lineage follows the MGM trailer's dates, which are the rights holder's own and fit the film's internal clock (Murphy dies in autumn, is rebuilt over New Year, and is on the street a few weeks later); they are reported, with screenshots, in a Science Fiction & Fantasy Stack Exchange answer, and the trailer itself could not be viewed for this research. The OCP police contract comes 'not long before' the film and is folded into the fork year.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours plus one privatisation: a corporation that owns a city's police and builds its officers. It follows the original film series, RoboCop (1987), RoboCop 2 (1990) and RoboCop 3 (1993), and not the 2014 remake (set in 2028, a separate continuity), the television series, the comics, or the 2023 game Rogue City. None of the films states a year; the first is pinned by an MGM trailer's dates (2029-2030) and the sequels by the release gaps between the films, so every story date is low confidence and the alternative placements are given in the divergence note. divergence.inUniverse: Day 1 (the film's closing caption); Thanksgiving falls in the first week
divergence.note: Contagion never shows a calendar year. It counts days from Day 2 to Day 135 and holds back Day 1, the handshake in Macau, for its last scene; Thanksgiving in the first week and Christmas about a month in fix the season. The atlas files Day 1 at about 20 November 2011, the week of the first Thanksgiving after the September 2011 release, as it files other undated present-day disasters at the first moment after their release. Reading the film as set during the winter it was shot in (Thanksgiving 2010) would move every story date back a year. The virus, MEV-1, is invented but modelled on Nipah; everything else, the CDC and its Epidemic Intelligence Service, the WHO, Homeland Security, is real.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Contagion (2011 film)
Scraps from the Loft: Contagion (2011) transcript (day captions; Thanksgiving and Christmas lines)

ending.why: By Day 135 the vaccine is reaching people, the death toll is falling and the looting has worn off, though 26 million are dead and the man who sold a fake cure is still broadcasting.

events.date: from March 1918 (first recorded case at Camp Funston, Kansas, 4 March 1918)
events.title: The 1918 influenza pandemic
events.description: Real history: an influenza that first shows itself in army camps in the last year of the First World War infects about a third of the world and kills something like 25 to 50 million people in three years.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish flu

events.note: Real-world background. Contagion's characters measure MEV-1 against it twice: a doctor notes that one per cent of the population died of the 1918 flu, and the blogger Alan Krumwiede observes that after it, 'people got rich'.
events.binWhy: A new disease spreads round the world on its own and kills on a civilisational scale.

facets.change: a world war → a pandemic that kills tens of millions

events.title: The United States vaccinates against a pandemic that never comes
events.description: Real history: after a soldier dies of a new swine flu at Fort Dix, the US government vaccinates about 43 million people against a feared repeat of 1918. The pandemic never arrives, cases of Guillain-Barre syndrome follow the shots, and the programme is suspended in December and never restarted.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 1976 swine flu outbreak

events.note: Real-world background. Krumwiede uses it against the MEV-1 vaccine on television: 'The swine flu vaccine killed people back in 1976.' It is the film's precedent for the distrust a crash vaccine programme has to overcome.
events.binWhy: A state puts a new vaccine into mass use.

facets.change: a feared pandemic → 43 million shots and a halted programme

events.title: Barry Marshall infects himself to prove a theory
events.description: Real history: an Australian doctor who cannot get his colleagues to accept that a bacterium causes stomach ulcers drinks a culture of it, falls ill, and proves his case. He shares the Nobel Prize for it in 2005.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Barry Marshall

events.note: Real-world background. Ally Hextall names him at the moment she injects herself with an untested MEV-1 vaccine and goes to sit with her infected father: 'Do you remember Dr. Barry Marshall?'
events.binWhy: A discovery about disease, proved by self-experiment, overturns what medicine believed.

facets.change: ulcers from stress → ulcers from a germ, proved on himself

events.title: Nipah virus passes from fruit bats through pigs to people
events.description: Real history: in Malaysia a virus carried by fruit bats reaches pig farms and then the farmers, causing 265 cases of encephalitis and 105 deaths; the outbreak is stopped by culling millions of pigs. The loss of the bats' forest habitat is one of the conditions that bring them to the farms.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nipah virus infection

events.note: Real-world background, and the model for MEV-1: Wikipedia records that the film's virus was based on a combination of Nipah and measles, and the last scene of the film, a bulldozed forest, a bat, a pig and a chef, restages the Nipah chain.
events.binWhy: A new disease emerges from animals and spreads on its own.

facets.change: a bat virus → an epidemic on the pig farms

events.date: late February 2003 (Metropole Hotel, Hong Kong); WHO global alert 12 March 2003
events.title: SARS flies out of a Hong Kong hotel
events.description: Real history: a new coronavirus that has been spreading in Guangdong since November 2002 reaches Hong Kong's Metropole Hotel, where one infected doctor passes it to guests who carry it to Singapore, Hanoi and Toronto. The WHO issues a global alert on 12 March; about 8,000 are infected and 774 die before it is contained in July.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2002-2004 SARS outbreak

events.note: Real-world background. Scott Z. Burns built the script on SARS and the 2009 flu (per Wikipedia), the film's outbreak begins in Hong Kong and is traced through hotel and casino footage, and a CDC official says the city is using 'the same protocols established for SARS'. The WHO doctor who first identified SARS, Carlo Urbani, died of it on 29 March 2003.
events.binWhy: A new disease emerges from animals and spreads round the world on its own.

facets.change: a Guangdong pneumonia → a global alert from one hotel

events.title: The H1N1 pandemic
events.description: Real history: a swine-origin influenza identified in Mexico and the United States in April spreads worldwide and is declared a pandemic by the WHO in June. It is milder than feared; the WHO counts about 18,000 confirmed deaths, later estimates are near 284,000, and the pandemic is declared over in August 2010.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2009 swine flu pandemic

events.note: Real-world background, and the most recent pandemic when the film was written and shot. An editor turns down Krumwiede's first story by starting to say 'after H1-', and a Minneapolis doctor's first thought is that the hospital has only seen measles and H1N1.
events.binWhy: A new disease spreads round the world on its own.

facets.change: a swine flu in Mexico → a declared pandemic

events.date: from about 20 November 2011 (Day 1) to the turn of the year (derived)
events.title: MEV-1 crosses into people and circles the world
events.description: A chef in a Macau casino who has just handled a pig that ate fruit dropped by a bat shakes hands with an American executive, and within days the virus is killing people in Hong Kong, Tokyo, London, Chicago and Minneapolis. It spreads by droplets and touch with a reproduction number of four and kills a quarter or more of those infected; by Christmas Chicago and Minnesota are sealed by the National Guard, pharmacies are stripped for a fake cure and the dead go to mass graves.
events.inUniverse: Day 1 to about Day 40

sources.title: Wikipedia: Contagion (2011 film)
Scraps from the Loft: Contagion (2011) transcript (day captions; Thanksgiving and Christmas lines)

events.note: The film counts days, not dates. Its anchors are Thanksgiving, which falls in the first week (a father tells his sick son he will be better by Thanksgiving; Homeland Security fears an attack timed for the holiday weekend), and Christmas, greeted about a month in. The film was shot between September 2010 and February 2011 and released in September 2011; the atlas files it at the first Thanksgiving after release, 24 November 2011, which puts Day 1 at about 20 November. The response steps of this year, isolation, school closures, the quarantine of Chicago, air travel grounded, 'social distancing' as 'our best defense', the fight over when to tell the public, would each be crackdown / emergency-rule in a chart with room for them; one event per year leaves only the disease itself.
events.binWhy: A new virus jumps from bats through a pig into people and spreads on its own; nobody made it, which the film sets against Homeland Security's first guess that it is a weapon.

facets.change: one handshake in Macau → a pandemic with a reproduction number of four

events.date: Day 131-135: about late March to early April 2012 (derived)
events.title: A vaccine, handed out by birthday lottery
events.description: A CDC scientist tests a candidate vaccine on herself, it works, and production is fast-tracked; by the time it is approved MEV-1 has killed 26 million people worldwide and 2.5 million in the United States. Doses are rationed by a televised lottery of birthdays and checked at checkpoints with bracelets, while a blogger who sold a fake forsythia cure to twelve million followers is arrested for fraud and bailed out by them.
events.inUniverse: Day 131 to Day 135

sources.title: Wikipedia: Contagion (2011 film)
Scraps from the Loft: Contagion (2011) transcript (day captions; Thanksgiving and Christmas lines)

events.note: Derived from the day captions: the vaccine is declared a success around Christmas (about Day 35) and the first batch is said to be about ninety days away; the lottery is held on Day 133. Counted from Day 1 at about 20 November 2011, Day 133 is about 1 April 2012. By Day 135 the looting has worn off and the death rate is falling.
events.binWhy: A new vaccine goes into mass use and turns the pandemic.

facets.change: no treatment → a vaccine, rationed by lottery

events.title: The Contagion team records messages for the real pandemic
events.description: Real history: in the first weeks of COVID-19 lockdowns, Matt Damon, Kate Winslet, Laurence Fishburne and Jennifer Ehle, with Steven Soderbergh and Scott Z. Burns, record public-service videos at home with scientists from Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health, among them W. Ian Lipkin, who advised the film.

sources.title: Columbia Mailman School of Public Health: Contagion team reunites to create coronavirus PSAs (27 March 2020)

events.note: Filed as the world's publication event in place of the release itself. The film opened at Venice on 3 September 2011 and in the United States on 9 September 2011, the same year as the fork, and the atlas allows one event per year. Wikipedia also records that the film became one of the most-watched titles in early 2020.
events.binWhy: Not a moment in the story: the film's makers speaking about the real pandemic, and standing in here for the 2011 release, which shares its year with the fork.

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: the world is ours, the institutions are real, and the fork is a single spillover in the film's own present. The story lasts about four and a half months, so its fiction occupies only two years, the outbreak and the vaccine; everything before them is the real history of outbreaks the film was built from (Nipah, SARS, H1N1) and the precedents its characters cite (1918, 1976, Barry Marshall). Follows the 2011 film only; the 2020 public-service videos are real-world messages, not story. Tiers: T3 holds the 1918, 1976, 1984 and 1998 background; T2 holds SARS, H1N1, the outbreak, the vaccine and the 2020 videos; T4 and T1 are empty because the film reaches back no further than the diseases it quotes and forward no further than the spring after.

lineages.title: The Andromeda Strain
lineages.creator: Michael Crichton

divergence.label: Merrick's paper on first contact by microbe
divergence.delta: Real: in 1962 the danger of contamination from space is a question for committees, and the only things coming back from orbit are spy-satellite film capsules. Fiction: a paper at Cold Spring Harbor persuades a Nobel laureate that the first contact will be an infection, and within five years the United States has a secret weapons programme sampling near space and a laboratory in Nevada waiting for what it brings back.
divergence.inUniverse: Summer 1962, Tenth Biological Symposium at Cold Spring Harbor
divergence.note: The novel is written as history and gives its own dates, from Merrick's paper in 1962 through the Wildfire file of 1965-66 to the five-day crisis of February 1967. Its scientists come with invented careers that reach back further (Stone is given the Nobel Prize for 1961), but a character's biography is not a history; the fork is filed at the first invented event from which the story's chain runs, which the novel itself says 'begun it all'.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course
Wikipedia: The Andromeda Strain

ending.why: Andromeda mutates into a form harmless to people and drifts away, but it is still mutating in the upper atmosphere, has just burned up a crewed capsule, and NASA has grounded crewed flight indefinitely because 'the decision is out of our hands'.

events.title: Scientists ask for rules against carrying germs between worlds
events.description: Real history: in the months after Sputnik, the geneticist Joshua Lederberg warns that spacecraft could carry Earth microbes to other worlds and bring foreign ones back. The US National Academy of Sciences passes a resolution on contamination, an international committee (CETEX) recommends sterilising spacecraft, and in 1959 COSPAR takes over the job.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Planetary protection
Wikipedia: Joshua Lederberg

events.note: Real-world background. The novel's own history begins here: it notes that by 1959 NASA had strict sterilisation rules for outbound probes, and has its Jeremy Stone, a young Nobel-winning bacteriologist, argue that the danger of returning craft was being ignored. Lederberg won the Nobel Prize in 1958; Wikipedia does not say Crichton modelled Stone on him.
events.binWhy: A scientific committee is formed that will set the rules for contamination in space.

facets.change: a space race → rules against contaminating other worlds

events.title: A capsule is caught coming back from orbit
events.description: Real history: the film capsule of Discoverer 14, a secret Corona reconnaissance satellite launched from Vandenberg, is snatched in mid-air over the Pacific by a C-119 aircraft, the first object ever recovered from orbit. Its photographs cover more of the Soviet Union than every U-2 flight before it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Discoverer 14

events.note: Real-world background. The novel's Scoop satellites use the same machinery: launched from Vandenberg into polar orbit for secrecy, and brought down by radio command for recovery by the military.
events.binWhy: A reconnaissance satellite returns its film from orbit: the machinery of watching people put to work.

facets.change: U-2 overflights → film caught in mid-air from orbit

events.title: Merrick predicts that first contact will be an infection
events.description: At a biology symposium at Cold Spring Harbor, the English biophysicist J. J. Merrick argues from the rarity of complex life that humanity's first contact with anything from space will be with a microorganism, and that it may well cause disease. The audience is amused; Jeremy Stone takes it seriously.
events.inUniverse: Tenth Biological Symposium, Cold Spring Harbor

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course

events.note: Stated in the novel, which calls Merrick the man who 'in his own way, begun it all'. Stone and his colleagues are given invented careers before this (Stone's Nobel Prize is dated 1961), but Merrick's paper is the first invented event from which the story's chain runs.
events.binWhy: A theory arrives, about what life from space will be, that the rest of the story turns on.

facets.change: first contact as a conversation → first contact as an infection

events.title: Project Scoop: a science satellite that is really a weapons search
events.description: The Army contracts the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, through NASA, to design satellites that will skim the edge of space and collect whatever organisms live there. The scientists are told it is pure research; its true purpose is to find new life forms for the biological-weapons programme at Fort Detrick.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course

events.note: Stated in the novel. The real Fort Detrick ran US biological-weapons research until 1969; Project Scoop and its aims are invented.
events.binWhy: The purpose of a programme is hidden from the scientists who build it and from the public.

facets.change: a curiosity-driven science satellite → a hidden hunt for germ weapons

events.date: 10 June 1964 (Stone's letter); construction ordered January 1965 and finished July 1966
events.title: Stone's letter to the President, and the Wildfire laboratory
events.description: Stone and four colleagues write to the President, in a letter patterned on Einstein's of 1939, that sterilising returning spacecraft can never be made safe, and ask for an underground laboratory to study anything that comes back, with a nuclear bomb to destroy it. Within a month they are an official committee; the Defense Department pays $22 million, and the Wildfire laboratory is built underground at Flatrock, Nevada, with a protocol to nuke any town where an alien organism lands.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course

events.note: All dates are stated in the novel: the letter is dated 10 June 1964, the Wildfire file records construction initiated by executive order in January 1965 and completed in July 1966. The novel places the letter's model in 1940; Einstein's letter to Roosevelt was dated August 1939.
events.binWhy: A secret body is founded to meet an extraterrestrial germ, and it will shape everything that happens when one arrives.

facets.change: a scientists' letter → an underground lab with a bomb inside

events.date: spring - December 1965 (the trial deaths follow on 1 March 1966)
events.title: Kalocin, a universal antibiotic, is found and buried
events.description: A drug company finds a compound that cures cancer by killing every single-celled organism in the body. When forty trial subjects are taken off it in March 1966, all forty die within six hours of diseases no one has seen, and the government suppresses all knowledge of the drug.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course

events.note: Stated in the novel as backstory, told at the height of the Wildfire crisis to explain why Stone refuses to use the drug on a dying colleague. The discovery is filed at 1965 because 1966 holds the first Scoop flights.
events.binWhy: A medical discovery arrives that the rest of the story will have to reckon with.

facets.change: an incurable cancer → a cure that opens the body to every germ

events.title: The Scoop satellites start to fly
events.description: Scoop I goes up from Vandenberg in March 1966 and comes down in a Georgia swamp with nothing but Earth germs. Two burn up on re-entry, two more bring back harmless skin bacteria, and Scoop VI, launched on New Year's Day 1967, returns a new organism that makes chickens ill.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course

events.note: Dates stated in the novel. The failures make the Army tighten sterilisation before each launch, which is why the organism Scoop VII brings back cannot be put down to contamination from Earth.
events.binWhy: Satellites go to the edge of space to collect life no one has found.

facets.change: a satellite programme on paper → six sampling flights to near space

events.date: February 1967 (Scoop VII launched on or about 5 February; down about two and a half days later)
events.title: Scoop VII comes down at Piedmont, Arizona
events.description: The Army brings a satellite down by radio in the desert, the town of Piedmont dies in hours with its blood clotted in its veins, and the Wildfire team is summoned to study the organism, Andromeda, with only an old man and a baby left alive. The President delays the order to bomb the town; Andromeda mutates, eats through the laboratory's seals and nearly sets off its bomb, then turns harmless and drifts out over the Pacific, while a crewed capsule, Andros V, burns up on re-entry.

sources.title: Michael Crichton, The Andromeda Strain (1969), full text as hosted for a Stony Brook astronomy course
Wikipedia: The Andromeda Strain

events.note: The novel says the launch date is classified but 'believed to be February 5, 1967', that the satellite orbited for two and a half days before it was brought down, and that it was February when the recovery team found the town; the crisis then lasts five days. The Andromeda organism is grown only in blood of normal acidity, which is why a drinker and a crying baby survive; it turns out to feed on energy, so the nuclear bomb Stone asked for would have fed it. In our February 1967 there is no Scoop programme, no Wildfire and no Piedmont.
events.binWhy: An organism collected by a weapons programme is brought down among people by accident and kills a town: released by people, not arising by itself.

facets.change: a recovered satellite → a dead town and an organism no one can stop

events.title: The Andromeda Strain is published
events.description: Michael Crichton publishes the novel under his own name, written as a declassified report of a five-day crisis, complete with teleprinter messages, computer printouts and pages 'deleted' from classified files.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Andromeda Strain

events.note: The foreword is signed 'M.C., Cambridge, Massachusetts, January 1969', and the book is framed as history, the story of a crisis two years before. It came out two months before Apollo 11, whose crew was quarantined in the real Lunar Receiving Laboratory that the novel mentions.
events.binWhy: Not a moment in the story: the original publication.

events.title: Robert Wise's film is released
events.description: The film adaptation keeps the story but moves it: the satellite comes down at Piedmont, New Mexico, one of the scientists becomes a woman, Dr. Ruth Leavitt, and the events are framed by testimony before a Senate committee.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Andromeda Strain (film)

events.note: A separate continuity, not followed here: the film's dates belong to its own present rather than to the novel's 1967.
events.binWhy: Not a moment in the story: the film adaptation.

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: the world is 1960s America, its space and weapons programmes are real (Vandenberg, JPL, Fort Detrick), and the fork is a scientific idea that the state turns into a secret programme. Follows Crichton's 1969 novel only. The 1971 film moves the story to New Mexico and its own present; the 2008 miniseries and Daniel H. Wilson's authorised 2019 sequel, The Andromeda Evolution, set fifty years later, are not charted. The crisis itself lasts five days, so the chain is mostly the invented history the novel builds for it. Tiers: T3 holds everything, from the real 1958-1960 background to the 1971 film; T4, T2 and T1 are empty because the novel reaches back only to the space age and forward only to its own epilogue.

lineages.title: Deep Impact
lineages.creator: Bruce Joel Rubin and Michael Tolkin (writers); Mimi Leder (director)

divergence.label: Leo Biederman photographs a comet
divergence.delta: Real: in May 1998 the Spaceguard goal of finding the big near-Earth asteroids is six years old and nothing on the catalogue is on course for Earth; the first module of the International Space Station is six months from launch. Fiction: a schoolboy's photograph shows a comet seven miles long that will hit the Earth, and the government hides it for a year while it builds a nuclear-armed spaceship with Russia.
divergence.inUniverse: 10 May 1998, Richmond, Virginia (per Wikipedia's reading of the opening)
divergence.note: Wikipedia's plot dates the discovery to 10 May 1998 and the main story to 1999; the film then says 'one year later', and the President gives the impact date as 'August 16, roughly a year from now', which puts it on 16 August 2000. I could not confirm the opening caption from a second source. The film was released on 8 May 1998, two days before its own fork date, so the release shares a year with the discovery and is not charted as a separate publication event. President Tom Beck means the film's politics had already parted from ours (Bill Clinton was president in 1998-2000) at a date the film never gives.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deep Impact (film)
Springfield! Springfield!: Deep Impact (1998) script (the President's announcement, the lottery and impact dates)

ending.why: The Messiah destroys the extinction-level fragment and the President opens the rebuilding of the Capitol; the Atlantic coasts are wrecked and millions are dead, but the world goes on.

events.title: Project Orion: a spaceship driven by atomic bombs
events.description: Real history: ARPA funds a General Atomics study, led by Ted Taylor with Freeman Dyson, of a spacecraft pushed along by nuclear explosions detonated behind it, fast enough for a crewed round trip to Mars. It never flies, and the 1963 ban on atmospheric tests ends it in 1964.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Project Orion (nuclear propulsion)

events.note: Real-world background. The film's Messiah is driven by 'Orion' boosters, which it credits to the Russians, and a newscaster explains the historical programme by name.
events.binWhy: A theory of how to move a ship with nuclear energy is worked out on paper.

facets.change: chemical rockets → a ship pushed by atomic bombs, on paper

events.title: The Alvarez team blames an impact for the dinosaurs
events.description: Real history: Luis and Walter Alvarez, Frank Asaro and Helen Michel report a layer of iridium at the end of the Cretaceous all over the world and argue that an asteroid impact caused the mass extinction 66 million years ago. The crater is later found at Chicxulub in Mexico.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Alvarez hypothesis

events.note: Real-world background. The idea the whole film rests on: an extinction-level event from the sky. A reporter at the President's announcement asks whether this is what killed the dinosaurs.
events.binWhy: A scientific discovery shows that the sky can end a world.

facets.change: a mysterious extinction → an impact from space

events.title: The Spaceguard Survey is proposed
events.description: Real history: a study requested by the US Congress produces the Spaceguard Survey report, which sets NASA the goal of finding 90 per cent of the near-Earth asteroids larger than a kilometre within a decade. The name comes from Arthur C. Clarke's 1973 novel Rendezvous with Rama.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spaceguard

events.note: Real-world background: the start of the organised watch for objects like the film's comet. The film's own sources include Clarke's 1993 novel The Hammer of God, about an asteroid aimed at Earth, though it is not credited.
events.binWhy: A programme is set up that will search the sky for objects on course for Earth.

facets.change: nobody watching → a survey of the sky for impactors

events.title: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 hits Jupiter
events.description: Real history: the pieces of a comet found by Carolyn and Eugene Shoemaker and David Levy strike Jupiter over six days, the largest with the energy of six million megatons and a dark spot almost as wide as the Earth. It is the first collision between solar-system bodies anyone has watched, and it turns impacts from theory into television.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9
Wikipedia: Deep Impact (film)

events.note: Real-world background. Gene and Carolyn Shoemaker were among the film's scientific consultants; the film's comet also breaks in two on the way in.
events.binWhy: An astronomical event shows the impact threat happening in real time.

facets.change: impacts as geology → an impact watched live

events.title: Two amateurs find comet Hale-Bopp
events.description: Real history: Alan Hale in New Mexico and Thomas Bopp, with a home-made telescope in the Arizona desert, independently find a comet that becomes visible to the naked eye for a record eighteen months. In March 1997 thirty-nine members of the Heaven's Gate cult kill themselves believing a spaceship travels behind it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Comet Hale-Bopp

events.note: Real-world background, and the pattern for Leo Biederman, the amateur whose photograph starts the film. When the President announces the comet, a producer in the newsroom shouts for 'the Hale-Bopp stand-ups'.
events.binWhy: An astronomical discovery made by amateurs.

facets.change: an empty patch of sky → the brightest comet in decades

events.title: Leo Biederman photographs a comet
events.description: At a school astronomy club's star party in Richmond, Virginia, a teenager notices an unknown object near the Big Dipper; the astronomer who works out that it will hit the Earth dies in a car crash racing to raise the alarm. The government learns of it anyway and keeps it secret, and within months the United States and Russia are building a spaceship in orbit to meet it.
events.inUniverse: Richmond, Virginia

sources.title: Wikipedia: Deep Impact (film)

events.note: The date is Wikipedia's reading of the film's opening, which the next scene follows with 'one year later'. It is two days after the film's own US release on 8 May 1998, which is why the release is not charted as a separate event: the atlas allows one event per year, and this year belongs to the fork. The US-Russian build of the Messiah, begun eight months before the President speaks, mirrors the International Space Station, whose first module was launched in November 1998.

facets.change: a smudge near the Big Dipper → a comet on course for Earth

events.date: 1999, about a year after the discovery (derived)
events.title: The President tells the world, and the Messiah flies
events.description: A television reporter who mistakes 'Ellie', E.L.E., for a cabinet secretary's mistress stumbles on the secret, and President Beck goes on air: a comet seven miles long may hit the Earth next August, and the United States and Russia have spent eight months building the Messiah in orbit to meet it. Two months later a crew of five Americans and a Russian launches to plant nuclear bombs in the comet.

The Messiah's landing on the comet and the failure of its bombs come some time in the following ten months, the President's own timescale, and are not dated.

events.date: 16 August 2000 (derived from 'August 16, roughly a year from now')
events.title: Biederman strikes the Atlantic; the Messiah stops Wolf
events.description: The Messiah's bombs split the comet in two instead of turning it; under martial law a computer lottery sends 800,000 Americans, with 200,000 chosen in advance, into caves in the Missouri limestone, and a last missile strike fails. The smaller piece hits the ocean off Cape Hatteras and a megatsunami drowns the East Coast as far as the Ohio and Tennessee valleys and reaches Europe and Africa, killing millions; the Messiah's crew flies into the larger piece and blows it apart before it can end all life.

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: the world is the late 1990s as they were, NASA, the space shuttle and US-Russian cooperation in orbit included, and the fork is one discovery in the film's own present. The 1998 release shares a year with the fork and is left out as a separate event. lineages.creator: Chris Sparling (writer); Ric Roman Waugh (director)

divergence.label: Comet Clarke
divergence.delta: Real: in 2021 the only two interstellar objects ever seen, 'Oumuamua and 2I/Borisov, have passed at a safe distance, and NASA's first deflection test, DART, launches in November. Fiction: an interstellar comet discovered only weeks earlier turns out to be a trail of fragments; one destroys Tampa, and two days later the largest ends civilisation.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated; Clarke is 'discovered only weeks ago'
divergence.note: Neither film gives a calendar year. The first is plainly set in its own present (smartphones, emergency alerts, Atlanta suburbs), was shot in 2019 and released in 2020; the atlas files the impact at 2021, the first year after release, as it does The Day After Tomorrow. The sequel's 'five years after' then lands in 2026. If the first film is read as set in 2020, every story date moves back one year.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Greenland (film)
Wikipedia: Greenland 2: Migration
Springfield! Springfield!: Greenland (2020) script ('discovered only weeks ago'; 'a long nine months underground')

ending.why: The Garritys reach the Clarke crater, which has healed into farmland under clear skies, and the survivors have a safe place to start again, though John dies within sight of it and much of the world is still ash and storms.

events.title: The United States builds Thule Air Base
events.description: Real history: under a defence agreement with Denmark, Operation Blue Jay builds an American air base in the far north-west of Greenland on a scale compared with the Panama Canal. In 1953 Denmark forcibly moves about 130 Inughuit from Old Thule to make room; the base is renamed Pituffik Space Base in 2023.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Pituffik Space Base

events.note: Real-world background. The film's refuge is a complex of bunkers near Thule Air Base, which is why the chosen are flown to Greenland at all.
events.binWhy: A permanent base is founded in remote territory on Earth.

facets.change: an Arctic coast → an American base in the ice

events.title: Camp Century: a town inside the ice sheet
events.description: Real history: the US Army digs 21 tunnels, three kilometres of them, into the ice sheet east of Thule and powers them with a portable nuclear reactor. Presented as a research station, it is a trial for Project Iceworm, a network of nuclear missile sites under the ice, and is abandoned in 1967 when the ice begins to crush it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Camp Century

events.note: Real-world background: the nearest thing in our history to the film's Greenland shelter, a place built under the ice to keep people alive through a catastrophe.
events.binWhy: A base is founded in new territory, under the ice sheet.

facets.change: an ice sheet → a nuclear-powered base inside it

events.title: NASA sets up its Planetary Defense Coordination Office
events.description: Real history: NASA creates an office to find and catalogue objects that could hit the Earth and to coordinate what would be done about one. Its first test, the DART spacecraft, launches in November 2021.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Planetary Defense Coordination Office

events.note: Real-world background. In the film no one has time to try: Clarke's fragments arrive within weeks of its discovery, and the only response is shelter.
events.binWhy: An agency is founded to watch for and answer impact threats.

facets.change: scattered surveys → an office for planetary defence

events.title: The first object from another star is seen passing through
events.description: Real history: Robert Weryk, using the Pan-STARRS telescope in Hawaii, finds 'Oumuamua, the first confirmed interstellar object, forty days after it has already swung past the Sun and while it is leaving the solar system.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 'Oumuamua

events.note: Real-world background. The film's Clarke is an interstellar comet; 'Oumuamua showed that such objects exist and that the first sign of one can come too late to do anything.
events.binWhy: An astronomical discovery: a visitor from another star.

facets.change: a solar system of its own objects → a visitor from another star

events.title: An amateur finds the first interstellar comet
events.description: Real history: Gennadiy Borisov, observing from Crimea with a telescope he built himself, finds 2I/Borisov, the first known comet from another star system. It passes no nearer than about 1.9 astronomical units from the Earth in December 2019.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2I/Borisov

events.note: Real-world background, found while Greenland was being shot. Clarke is an interstellar comet discovered only weeks before its closest approach; Borisov was the first real one, and it stayed far away.
events.binWhy: An astronomical discovery: a comet from another star.

facets.change: interstellar objects as rocks → a comet from another star

events.title: Greenland is released
events.description: The film opens in Belgium in July 2020 and reaches American audiences on video on demand in December, its cinema release lost to the COVID-19 pandemic.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Greenland (film)

events.note: Its sequel, Greenland 2: Migration, was released on 9 January 2026 in the United States; that year is taken by the sequel's story, so its release is not charted separately.
events.binWhy: Not a moment in the story: the original release.

events.date: 2021, undated; the impacts come over about three days (derived)
events.title: Comet Clarke breaks up over the Earth
events.description: An interstellar comet discovered only weeks before is due to pass close; instead a fragment expected to fall near Bermuda vaporises Tampa, and the government reveals that the largest piece, nine miles wide, will strike in two days. Selected families are summoned to air bases for flights to bunkers in Greenland while mobs storm the gates, and the fragment that hits Western Europe devastates civilisation around the world.
events.inUniverse: Clarke 'discovered only weeks ago'

sources.title: Wikipedia: Greenland (film)
Springfield! Springfield!: Greenland (2020) script ('discovered only weeks ago'; 'a long nine months underground')

events.note: Greenland shows no calendar date or season. It was shot in 2019 and released in 2020; following the atlas's rule for undated present-day disasters (the first year after release, as with The Day After Tomorrow), it is filed at 2021. Read as set in its own present, every story date would move back a year.
events.binWhy: A cosmic disaster brings down civilisation across the planet, not just in the places it hits.

facets.change: a comet passing close → a world ended in three days

events.title: The blast doors open after nine months
events.description: The ash is mostly gone and there is no sign of radiation, so the people in the Greenland bunkers open the doors onto a ruined, silent landscape and hear birds. Radio stations answer from Fairbanks, New Delhi, Sao Paulo, Moscow, Buenos Aires and Beirut: others have survived, and the sky is clearing.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Greenland (film)
Springfield! Springfield!: Greenland (2020) script ('discovered only weeks ago'; 'a long nine months underground')

events.note: Nine months after an undated impact filed at 2021 falls in 2021 or 2022, depending on the month of the impact, which the film never gives; it is filed at 2022, where it falls for any impact after March.
events.binWhy: A jump forward shows what became of the world: survivors everywhere, and a sky starting to clear.

facets.change: nine months underground → radio contact and a clearing sky

events.title: Migration: from the collapsing bunker to the crater
events.description: Five years on, electromagnetic storms, fallout, falling debris and earthquakes still wrack the planet; a quake and a tsunami destroy the Greenland bunker and kill most of those in it. The Garritys cross a ruined Britain and a dry English Channel to the impact crater in southern France, rumoured to be farmed and defended by the military, and find it has healed into fertile land under clear skies; John dies of his wounds within sight of it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Greenland 2: Migration

events.note: Greenland 2: Migration opens 'five years after the impact'; counted from 2021, that is 2026, the year of the sequel's own release (January 2026), which is therefore not charted separately.
events.binWhy: A new refuge on Earth: the survivors abandon one shelter and reach the place where the world has started to grow again.

facets.change: a Greenland bunker → a farmed crater in France

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: the world is ours, the American emergency machinery (Homeland Security alerts, air force bases, FEMA camps) is real, and the fork is one comet in the films' present. The first film's story lasts about three days plus a nine-month coda, so the chain before the fork is the real background the films build on: the American base at Thule, the under-ice Camp Century, NASA's planetary-defence office and the first two interstellar visitors. Follows Greenland (2020) and Greenland 2: Migration (2026). Tiers: T3 holds Thule and Camp Century; T2 holds everything from 2016 to 2026; T4 and T1 are empty.

divergence.label: Satnam Tsurutani's neutrinos
divergence.delta: Real: in 2009 the Sun has just begun a new sunspot cycle, which will prove the weakest in a century, and the 2012 phenomenon is a fringe belief NASA scientists spend years debunking. Fiction: an Indian astrophysicist finds that solar neutrinos are heating the Earth's core, and the governments that learn of it have three years to hide the end of the world and build arks for a chosen few.
divergence.inUniverse: 2009 (opening caption), a copper mine in Jharkhand, India
divergence.note: 2012 is one of the few disaster films that captions its own years: its sections are headed 2009, 2010, 2011 and 2012, and the flood recedes twenty-seven days after the end. The fork year is the film's release year, so the release is represented by the November 2008 trailer and website instead.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2012 (film)
The Movie Spoiler: 2012 (2009) (the 2009, 2010, 2011 and 2012 sections)

ending.why: Twenty-seven days after billions die the waters are receding and the arks, their gates opened to the people left outside, sail for a risen Africa to begin again.

events.title: Hapgood's theory that the Earth's crust can slide
events.description: Real history: the American historian Charles Hapgood publishes The Earth's Shifting Crust, with a foreword by Albert Einstein, arguing that the whole outer shell of the planet has slipped over its interior many times. Geologists largely ignore it, and plate tectonics replaces it within a decade.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Charles Hapgood
Springfield! Springfield!: 2012 (2009) script

events.note: Real-world background. The film makes Hapgood right: the radio prophet Charlie Frost explains 'Earth Crust Displacement' by name and date ('In 1958, Professor Charles Hapgood...'), and the disaster is exactly that.
events.binWhy: A theory about the planet's surface that the film's whole catastrophe turns on.

facets.change: fixed continents → a crust that can slide

events.title: A Maya scholar reads the end of the Long Count as Armageddon
events.description: Real history: in The Maya, the archaeologist Michael D. Coe suggests that the Maya expected 'Armageddon' to overtake the world at the completion of the thirteenth b'ak'tun of their calendar, a date later computed as 21 December 2012. Later scholars reject the reading, but it becomes the seed of a modern prophecy.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2012 phenomenon

events.note: Real-world background. The film's calendar comes from the 2012 phenomenon that grew out of readings like Coe's; a news report in the film mentions a mass suicide at Tikal by believers in 'the Mayan calendar', which it says predicts the end of time on the 21st of December.
events.binWhy: A scholarly reading of an ancient society's calendar, on which the modern prophecy the film uses rests.

facets.change: a calendar cycle → a date for the end of the world

events.title: Super-Kamiokande shows that neutrinos have mass
events.description: Real history: the Super-Kamiokande detector in a Japanese mine announces the first evidence that neutrinos change type in flight, which means they have mass. The discovery wins the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Super-Kamiokande

events.note: Real-world background. The film's science rests on neutrinos behaving in a new way: its disaster begins when an astrophysicist in an Indian copper mine finds solar neutrinos heating the Earth's core, which real neutrinos cannot do.
events.binWhy: A discovery about matter that the film's invented physics borrows from.

facets.change: massless neutrinos → neutrinos that change type and carry mass

events.title: Forecasters predict a violent solar maximum
events.description: Real history: NCAR's Mausumi Dikpati predicts that the next sunspot cycle will be 30 to 50 per cent stronger than the last, with a maximum around 2012, and NASA publicises the forecast as a 'solar storm warning'. The cycle turns out to be the weakest in about a century, peaking in April 2014.

sources.title: Space Daily: Solar Storm Warning (13 March 2006)
Wikipedia: Solar cycle 24
Wikipedia: 2012 phenomenon

events.note: Real-world background. NASA's David Morrison later traced the doomsday pages' solar-storm fears partly to the 2006 headline. The film's scientists warn of 'the biggest solar climax in recorded history'.
events.binWhy: An astronomical forecast of a threat from the Sun.

facets.change: a routine solar cycle → a forecast of the strongest in decades

events.title: The first trailer, and the Institute for Human Continuity
events.description: Sony releases the first trailer for 2012, ending with an invitation to 'find out the truth' by searching the web for the year, and launches the website of a fictional Institute for Human Continuity where visitors can register for a rescue lottery. A NASA scientist who receives more than a thousand letters from people who believe it condemns the campaign.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2012 (film)

events.note: Filed as the world's publication event in place of the release itself: the film opened on 13 November 2009, the same year as its fork (the opening scene is captioned 2009), and the atlas allows one event per year.
events.binWhy: Not a moment in the story: the film's marketing, standing in for the 2009 release, which shares its year with the fork.

events.title: Neutrinos are found heating the Earth's core
events.description: In a copper mine in Jharkhand, the Indian astrophysicist Satnam Tsurutani shows an American geologist, Adrian Helmsley, that a new kind of neutrino from a burst of solar activity is heating the planet's core. Helmsley takes it to the White House.
events.inUniverse: Jharkhand, India

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2012 (film)
The Movie Spoiler: 2012 (2009) (the 2009, 2010, 2011 and 2012 sections)

events.note: The film captions its first scenes 2009, the year of its own release (13 November 2009). Nothing earlier in the film departs from our history.
events.binWhy: A discovery about the planet itself that dooms it.

facets.change: a quiet mine → a planet whose core is heating

events.title: At the G8, the world's leaders agree to build arks in secret
events.description: President Wilson tells his fellow heads of state at a G8 summit that the world will soon end, and forty-six nations led by the G8 and China begin building nine arks in the Tibetan Himalayas, disguised as a dam project. The public is told nothing, and part of the cost is met by selling seats to the very rich at a billion euros each.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2012 (film)
The Movie Spoiler: 2012 (2009) (the 2009, 2010, 2011 and 2012 sections)
Springfield! Springfield!: 2012 (2009) script
Wikipedia: 36th G8 summit

events.note: The film captions the summit 2010 and later recalls it as 'British Columbia, 2010'. The real 2010 G8 summit met at Huntsville, Ontario, on 25-26 June 2010; the film moves it west.
events.binWhy: Governments that know the world is ending agree to hide it and save a chosen few.

facets.change: a scientist's warning → a secret pact and nine arks

events.title: The Mona Lisa is swapped for a copy
events.description: The Louvre's Mona Lisa is replaced by a replica that only infrared analysis could tell apart, and the original goes into safekeeping with selections from the British Museum and the Hermitage for the arks. The Louvre's director is later killed by a car bomb in Paris before a press conference, and the White House chief of staff defends the killing of anyone who tried to talk.

events.note: The swap is captioned 2011. The director's death is reported on the news in the film's 2012 section; the chief of staff's 'How do you think we kept it a secret?' comes during the evacuation.
events.binWhy: The world's heritage is quietly removed and replaced with fakes so that no one will know why.

facets.change: the real Mona Lisa → a replica on the wall

events.date: December 2012 (the film ties the end to 21 December; the day itself is not captioned)
events.title: The crust slides, and billions die
events.description: Yellowstone erupts, California slides into the Pacific, and as the Earth's crust shifts on its core, earthquakes and a megatsunami kill billions, among them the President, who stays in Washington; his chief of staff makes himself acting commander-in-chief. At the arks the loading gates are shut on the many people still outside until Helmsley persuades the surviving leaders to let them in.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2012 (film)
Springfield! Springfield!: 2012 (2009) script

events.note: The film captions its main story 2012 and ties the disaster to the winter solstice ('12-21-12', in Charlie Frost's words), though the catastrophe comes sooner than the scientists first predicted and the day itself is not captioned.
events.binWhy: A cosmic and geological disaster brings down civilisation everywhere at once.

facets.change: a world of nations → nine arks on a drowned planet

events.title: The waters fall and Africa rises
events.description: Twenty-seven days later the floods are receding, and the arks turn toward the Cape of Good Hope: Africa has risen, the Drakensberg are now the highest mountains on Earth, and the survivors set out to build new homes there.
events.inUniverse: Day 27 after the disaster

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2012 (film)

events.note: Wikipedia's plot gives 'twenty-seven days later'. The franchise's fan wiki describes the closing caption as restarting the calendar at year one; I could not open that page to confirm the wording. Counted from late December 2012, day 27 falls in January 2013.
events.binWhy: Survivors of a drowned world set out to found new homes on the only continent left.

facets.change: a drifting ark → a new continent to settle

lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: the world is ours, its leaders are the G8, and the fork is a discovery in the film's own present that governments decide to hide. The film dates itself year by year, so the fiction fills 2009-2013 with one event each; before the fork are the real ideas it stitches together, Hapgood's crust displacement, the reading of the Maya calendar that became the 2012 phenomenon, real neutrino physics and a real forecast of a violent solar maximum. Follows the 2009 film. Tiers: T3 holds the 1958, 1966 and 1998 background; T2 holds 2006-2013; T4 and T1 are empty.

lineages.title: Snow Crash
lineages.creator: Neal Stephenson

divergence.label: America is franchised
divergence.delta: Real: 2000 - the dollar is the world's reserve currency, the federal budget is in surplus and the web is five years old. Fiction: hyperinflation has made the trillion-dollar bill small change, the federal government has retreated into armed compounds, and the country is run by franchise-nations, burbclaves and private highways.
divergence.note: Snow Crash never gives a year for its present or for the collapse behind it: Wikipedia describes it as the 21st century, 'an unspecified number of years after a worldwide economic collapse'. The present is placed at about 2005 from the characters' ages (a thirty-year-old whose father was a prisoner of war in 1945; a Vietnam veteran running the Mafia). The fork follows the Neuromancer precedent: a round year before that present in which the collapse has plainly happened. Both years are placements, not dates in the text.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Snow Crash
Reactor: An Explosion of Ideas - Snow Crash (on its setting, the Raft and the USS Enterprise)

ending.why: Rife is dead, the counter-spell has broken his hold on the Raft and the hackers are safe, even though the franchised America around them is unchanged.

events.title: Japan occupies Attu and Kiska
events.description: Japanese forces land on the western Aleutians, the only incorporated US territory occupied in the war. The Aleuts of Attu are shipped to Japan as prisoners, and about forty per cent of them die there. The United States removes the other Aleut villages to camps in southeast Alaska, where 85 of 831 die.

Newspaper Rock: Raven in Snow Crash (the Aleutian grievance)

events.note: Real history. The novel builds on it through Raven, the Aleut harpooner, who has never forgiven the United States for how it handled the invasion (Newspaper Rock's reading of the novel). The historical figures are from Wikipedia's campaign article.
events.binWhy: A power's territory is invaded and occupied, and its native people are removed.

facets.change: island villages → an occupied chain and interned Aleuts

events.title: Nagasaki
events.description: The second atomic bomb destroys Nagasaki. In the novel, two men in a prisoner-of-war camp outside the city survive it: Hiro Protagonist's father and Raven's father. The swords Hiro carries were won from the Japanese officer who was about to execute his father when the flash came.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
Shmoop: Raven (Dmitri Ravinoff) character analysis - father 'nuked by the United States twice'

events.note: The date is history. The novel's use of it (both fathers in the camp outside Nagasaki, the swords taken from the officer) is reported by study guides (Shmoop), which I have not checked against the text. It is the first of the two times, in Raven's telling, that the United States 'nuked' his father.
events.binWhy: A nuclear weapon kills a city.

facets.change: a city → a crater, and two fathers with a grudge and a sword

events.title: USS Enterprise is commissioned
events.description: The US Navy commissions Enterprise, its first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier. In the novel a decommissioned Enterprise is bought by the media baron L. Bob Rife and becomes the centre of the Raft, a huge flotilla of Eurasian refugees drifting towards the West Coast.

sources.title: Wikipedia: USS Enterprise (CVN-65)
Reactor: An Explosion of Ideas - Snow Crash (on its setting, the Raft and the USS Enterprise)

events.note: The commissioning date is history; the real ship was decommissioned on 3 February 2017, long after the novel. Wikipedia's plot summary identifies Rife's yacht as the former nuclear carrier CVN-65.
events.binWhy: A new kind of war machine enters service; the novel turns it into a refugee city.

facets.change: oil-fired carriers → a carrier that never needs to refuel

events.title: Cannikin, under Amchitka
events.description: The United States sets off its largest underground nuclear test, the warhead for the Spartan anti-ballistic missile, beneath Amchitka in the Aleutians, over protests from Alaska and Canada. In the novel it is the second time the United States 'nuked' Raven's father, and the root of Raven's plan to take revenge on America with a nuclear warhead.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cannikin (1971 underground test on Amchitka)
Shmoop: Raven (Dmitri Ravinoff) character analysis - father 'nuked by the United States twice'

events.note: The test and its date are history. Shmoop's summary of the novel gives 1972 for the Amchitka blast, which may be the book's own slip or the guide's; the real Cannikin shot was on 6 November 1971, and that is the date used.
events.binWhy: A thermonuclear warhead meant to defend against a nuclear attack is tested.

facets.change: a remote island → the site of the largest underground blast

events.title: Snow Crash is published
events.description: Bantam publishes Neal Stephenson's third novel. It coins the word 'metaverse' for a shared virtual world that the internet might become.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Snow Crash

events.note: Real-world publication (Bantam, June 1992).
events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: America is franchised
events.description: After a worldwide economic collapse, hyperinflation leaves trillion-dollar bills nearly worthless. The federal government cedes most of its power and territory and retreats into its own compounds. Los Angeles is no longer part of the United States, and the country is run by franchise-nations, gated burbclaves, private highways, mercenary armies and a Mafia that delivers pizza.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Snow Crash
Reactor: An Explosion of Ideas - Snow Crash (on its setting, the Raft and the USS Enterprise)

events.note: Undated in the novel: 'an unspecified number of years' before the present. Following the precedent of the Neuromancer entry, the fork is placed at a round year before the present in which the change has plainly already happened. 2000 is a placeholder, not a date the book gives.
events.binWhy: Corporations and franchises end up running what the state used to run.

facets.change: a federal republic → a patchwork of franchise-nations

events.title: Snow Crash is released
events.description: A bitmap called Snow Crash, shown to hackers in the Metaverse, crashes their brains as well as their computers, while a drug version spreads through the Raft. L. Bob Rife means to use it, and an ancient Sumerian language that works on the brain like code, to control people. With Juanita's help the counter-spell, the nam-shub of Enki, is read out on the Raft and Rife's control breaks. Hiro neutralises the digital virus at a Metaverse concert, and Rife is killed trying to escape on his private jet.

events.note: The novel gives no year. Hiro is about thirty and his father was a prisoner of war in 1945, and Uncle Enzo is a Vietnam veteran. Reactor notes that these ages 'root the book in the time when it was written'. Together they put the present somewhere around 2005-2015; I use 2005.
events.binWhy: An attack carried through a computer network, aimed at the people who build it.

facets.change: a virtual world → a weapon that crashes the minds of its builders

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because its world is late-20th-century America pushed one step further: the state dissolves into franchises and a virtual world becomes the place where power moves. It follows the 1992 novel only (The Diamond Age is its own lineage). The novel dates almost nothing, so the chain is short on purpose: four real events the novel builds its characters on (the Aleutians 1942, Nagasaki 1945, the Enterprise 1961, Cannikin 1971), the publication, the placed fork and the story's present. Seven entries in all, six of them story events; I did not pad it with invented dates. Tier coverage is T3 for the real history and publication (1942-1992) and T2 for the fork and present (2000-2005). There is no T4 because the Sumerian past the plot turns on is myth, not a dated event, and no T1 because the story never leaves its own decade.

lineages.title: The Diamond Age
lineages.creator: Neal Stephenson

divergence.label: A stolen Primer reaches a four-year-old
divergence.delta: Real: 2060 is thirty-four years from now. Fiction: nations have given way to phyles, tribes chosen by culture; every home has a matter compiler fed atoms by a Feed the Neo-Victorians control; and the Chinese coast is divided into leased enclaves on artificial diamond islands.
divergence.note: The Diamond Age dates nothing. Its world has plainly diverged well before its first scene: nation-states have dissolved into phyles and nanotechnology is universal. But no earlier year can be fixed, so, as in the Blade Runner entry, the fork is the earliest point the story lets us place. That is placed at about 2060 through Miss Matheson, the aged ex-skateboarder usually read as Snow Crash's Y.T. Low confidence throughout.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Diamond Age
Wikiquote: The Diamond Age (Miss Matheson: 'I used to be a thrasher')

ending.why: The Coastal Republic has fallen, the Seed that could end the Feed's monopoly is nearly within the Celestial Kingdom's reach, and Nell's new tribe of Primer-raised girls has just been born; the book stops before any of them shows what it will become.

events.title: The Treaty of Nanking
events.description: The First Opium War ends with Qing China ceding Hong Kong Island to Britain and opening five ports to foreign trade and residence. It is the first of the foreign enclaves on the China coast that the novel's Leased Territories deliberately echo.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Treaty of Nanking
Wikipedia: The Diamond Age

events.note: Real history. The novel's Leased Territories around Shanghai, and the anti-foreign rising that ends it, replay the century of treaty ports and concessions that began here.
events.binWhy: A defeated state cedes territory and opens its ports to the victors.

facets.change: a closed coast → ports held by foreigners

events.title: The Boxer Uprising
events.description: The Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists rises in north China against foreigners and Christians and besieges the foreign legations in Beijing, before an eight-nation army crushes it. The novel's Fists of Righteous Harmony take the name and stage the rising again, this time against the Feed.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Boxer Rebellion
Wikipedia: The Diamond Age

events.note: Real history (September 1899 to September 1901). The Diamond Age's Fists are a deliberate replay: an anti-Western wing of the Confucian Celestial Kingdom rising against the foreign-run Feed.
events.binWhy: An armed rising against the foreign powers that hold the coast.

facets.change: resentment of foreign enclaves → an armed rising against them

events.title: Engines of Creation
events.description: K. Eric Drexler's book proposes molecular assemblers that build anything atom by atom. With Ralph Merkle's case for diamond as the material they would make most easily, it is the idea the novel treats as settled engineering. Both men are named in the novel.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Engines of Creation
Wikipedia: The Diamond Age

events.note: Real history. Wikipedia on the novel notes that Drexler and Merkle receive an honorary mention in it, and takes the title from Merkle's line about a coming 'Diamond Age'.
events.binWhy: A theory of building matter atom by atom, which the novel's world turns on.

events.title: The Diamond Age is published
events.description: Neal Stephenson's fourth novel, subtitled 'A Young Lady's Illustrated Primer', appears. It wins the 1996 Hugo and Locus awards.

events.title: A stolen Primer reaches a four-year-old
events.description: A Neo-Victorian Equity Lord commissions an interactive book to raise his granddaughter to think for herself. Its engineer, John Percival Hackworth, secretly compiles a second copy for his own daughter and is mugged on the way home. The copy ends up with Nell, a four-year-old with no tribe in the slums of the Leased Territories.

lineages.creator: Charles Stross

divergence.label: Uploaded lobsters ask for asylum
divergence.delta: Real: 2013 - smartphones everywhere, deep learning just starting to work, and no one has copied a living nervous system into a computer. Fiction: an uploaded lobster brain phones an Amsterdam idea broker asking to defect, and gets a job in space.

divergence.note: Accelerando dates its chapters by decade in the narrator's interludes ('the second decade', 'the fourth decade', 'decade the sixth') but never gives the opening year. Stross wrote on 27 May 2013 that it was 'roughly the year in which Accelerando was set', so the fork is placed there. The internal count ('eight years ago' on 'the eve of the third decade') would put it at 2011-12. The first thing the novel adds to our world is machine minds that can bargain for themselves, so that is the fork.

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs here because it starts in a recognisable Amsterdam of the 2010s, within a year or two of the real calendar, and its future is our century continued with one addition: minds that can be copied and improved. That addition compounds decade by decade into a singularity. It follows the novel as published in 2005 (the nine Asimov's stories revised into one text), and all dates come from the narrator's decade-by-decade interludes. Tier coverage is T2 for everything, from the 2001 magazine story to the last chapter in about 2265. There is no T4 or T3 because the novel's past is simply ours, and no T1 because its last chapter stops in the 22nd to 24th century.

lineages.title: New York 2140
lineages.creator: Kim Stanley Robinson

divergence.label: The First Pulse: the sea rises ten feet in a decade
divergence.delta: Real: in 2017, when the book appeared, the IPCC's 2013 assessment put this century's likely sea-level rise at about 1.5 to 3 feet, and a 2016 study had only just argued that Antarctic ice cliffs could collapse fast enough to make multi-metre rise thinkable. Fiction: in the mid-century, collapses in the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets raise the global sea by ten feet in about ten years, and every coastal city on Earth floods at once.
divergence.inUniverse: The First Pulse. The book gives it as history told by its 'citizen' narrator, not as a dated scene; reviewers place it in the 2050s or the 2060s.
divergence.note: The novel dates its catastrophes by decade and through its chorus-narrator, not by year, and its readers disagree by a decade. Robert Kopp, a Rutgers sea-level scientist writing in March 2017, puts the First Pulse in the 2050s; Mal Warwick's review puts it in the 2060s; A Green Man Review says 'about 2060'. Robinson's own description on Living on Earth (ten years of fast rise, then about thirty quiet years, then a worse second pulse) fits Kopp's 2050s best if the Second Pulse begins in the 2080s. The fork is filed at 2050, the start of the earliest decade any source gives. Nothing earlier in the book is known to contradict our history: its political argument is built on the real 2008 crash and its drowned Manhattan on Hurricane Sandy.

ending.why: After the hurricane and the debt strike, the Fed's bailout comes with conditions that make the Treasury majority owner of the banks, a wave of radical Democrats including Charlotte Armstrong is elected, and the proceeds go to health care, education and housing, though the narrator warns that such gains are transient and capitalism has only been squeezed.

events.title: Lehman Brothers fails and the banks are bailed out
events.description: Real history: a housing bubble built on speculative lending bursts, Lehman Brothers files the largest bankruptcy in US history, and Congress authorises $700 billion to buy toxic assets and bank stock. Robinson wrote New York 2140 in response to this crash, and the novel's plot is built to answer it: a second crash in which the public does not simply pay.

events.binWhy: A speculative bubble bursts and throws the economy into years of recession; the bailout that follows is what the novel sets out to undo.

facets.change: a housing bubble → a banking collapse paid for by the public

events.title: Hurricane Sandy floods Lower Manhattan
events.description: Real history: Sandy comes ashore near Atlantic City and drives a storm surge into New York Harbor that floods streets, subway lines and road tunnels in Lower Manhattan. It kills 160 people in the United States and does about $65 billion of damage. It is the flood the novel extrapolates into a permanently drowned downtown.

The death toll is modest for this bin; it is filed here because it is the event that made a flooded Manhattan a thing people had seen.

events.title: A model says Antarctica could add more than a metre by 2100
events.description: Real history: Robert DeConto and David Pollard publish a model in Nature in which Antarctic ice shelves break up and the ice cliffs behind them collapse under their own weight. Under high emissions the continent alone adds more than a metre of sea level by 2100 and more than fifteen by 2500. It was the most discussed climate paper of the year, and the kind of fast ice-sheet collapse the novel's two Pulses dramatise.
