events.binWhy: An attack on the financial system carried out through its own networks.

facets.change: a market no one can touch → a hack, and two coders gone

events.title: Hurricane Fyodor, and the everybody strike
events.description: Hurricane Fyodor batters New York for three days, destroys the intertidal zone and drives thousands of homeless people into a refugee camp in Central Park; weeks later, with luxury towers standing empty, the camp riots. The Householders' Union calls on everyone to stop paying mortgages, rents and insurance, the intertidal bubble and the banks collapse, and this time the bailout makes the Treasury their majority shareholder while a wave of radical Democrats is voted into Congress.
events.inUniverse: Hurricane Fyodor; the Householders' Union's debt strike

sources.title: Progress in Political Economy: Everybody strike! The urban environmental politics of New York 2140 (a 2142 hurricane; the strike; the Treasury as majority shareholder)
Living on Earth: New York 2140 (Hurricane Fyodor and the householders' union)

events.note: The PPE Sydney essay and Grokipedia put the hurricane in 2142; one search summary gave 2141. The strike follows within weeks, and the election and nationalisation follow from it, so hurricane and strike are filed together at 2142. A US congressional election falls in an even year, which fits 2142.
events.binWhy: A mass of unarmed people withhold payment together and force a change in who owns the banks; it is a strike, not an armed revolt.

facets.change: bailouts for the banks → the banks owned by the public

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours, with our banks, our Fed and our 2008, until the ice sheets give way in mid-century; the rest of the history follows from two floods and one old financial habit. It follows the novel alone. Tier coverage is T2 throughout, from the 2008 crash to the strike of 2142. There is no T3 or T4 because the book's history begins with the crash it answers, and no T1 because it never leaves the twenty-second century. The fork and both Pulses are dated only by decade.

lineages.title: The Water Knife
lineages.creator: Paolo Bacigalupi

divergence.label: The drought never breaks, and the river states arm
divergence.delta: Real: in 2016 the Colorado River basin is years into drought and drawing down its groundwater (a NASA satellite study found 65 cubic kilometres of fresh water lost from 2004 to 2013), and the seven states still settle shortages through compacts, courts and negotiated cuts. Fiction: the drought never ends. Texas dries into a failed state whose people flee west, other states close their borders to them, and Nevada, Arizona and California fight over the river with lawyers, private contractors and sabotage.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated: the novel is set in an unnamed near future after years of the 'Big Daddy Drought'
divergence.note: The novel states no year for its present or for its backstory. The fork is filed at 2016, the first year after the May 2015 publication, as the earliest year the fiction could leave our history; it is a floor, not a date the book gives. Bacigalupi has said the book grew out of the 2011 Texas drought, when Governor Rick Perry called for prayers for rain, which is why the novel's Texan refugees include a sect called the Merry Perrys. Everything the novel tells as backstory (Texas's collapse, the closed state lines, California's attacks on Arizona's water) must fall between this floor and the novel's present.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Water Knife
Colorado Public Radio: Bacigalupi ten years after The Water Knife (the 2011 Texas drought as the starting point)
NASA: Satellite study reveals parched U.S. West using up underground water (24 July 2014)

ending.why: The senior Pima water rights that could have saved Phoenix end up with Catherine Case and Las Vegas after Maria shoots Lucy to buy her own way in, and the book closes on Las Vegas helicopters coming in over a dying Arizona.

events.title: The Colorado River Compact divides the river
events.description: Real history: seven states meet at Bishop's Lodge near Santa Fe and split the Colorado River between an Upper and a Lower Basin, 7.5 million acre-feet a year each. The split assumed a flow the river does not reliably deliver, so the river was over-allocated from the start. Arizona refused to ratify until 1944.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Colorado River Compact

events.note: Real-world background. The whole plot of the novel is a fight over paper rights to water, and the Compact is the first and largest of those papers. Later tree-ring studies put the river's average flow at roughly 13 to 14.3 million acre-feet, well below the 16.4 the negotiators assumed.
events.binWhy: Rival states sign a pact dividing a shared river, which ends one quarrel and sets the terms for every later one.

facets.change: a contested river → a divided and over-allocated one

events.title: Arizona sends the National Guard against a California dam
events.description: Real history: Governor Benjamin Moeur declares martial law and sends about a hundred Arizona National Guardsmen, some on borrowed ferryboats nicknamed the 'Arizona Navy', to stop work on Parker Dam, which would divert water to Southern California. No shots are fired, but construction is suspended until the federal government re-authorises the dam in 1935.

sources.title: Earth Magazine: November 10, 1934: Arizona declares war against California at Parker Dam

events.note: Real-world background: the one time the river states actually sent troops. In the novel, state militias and National Guard units hold the borders and the river, which is this standoff made permanent.
events.binWhy: Two states face each other with troops over a river and stop short of shooting.

facets.change: a legal quarrel → troops on the river

events.date: 30 September 1935 (dedicated; Lake Mead began filling 1 February 1935)
events.title: Hoover Dam is dedicated and Lake Mead fills
events.description: Real history: President Roosevelt dedicates the dam in Black Canyon, and the reservoir behind it becomes the store of water for Nevada, Arizona and California. Las Vegas grows on its intakes. In the novel the lake has shrunk inside its white 'bathtub rings', and whoever controls it controls the Lower Basin.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hoover Dam

events.note: Real-world background. Construction ran from 1931 to 1936; the dedication is used as the date.
events.binWhy: A piece of engineering that makes desert cities possible and ties them to one reservoir.

facets.change: a flooding wild river → a managed reservoir for three states

events.title: The Supreme Court settles Arizona v. California
events.description: Real history: after decades of dispute, the Court decides how much of the Lower Colorado each state may take, rules that the Secretary of the Interior allocates the water, and recognises reserved water rights for Indian reservations along the river. The rights of tribes, older than most state claims, are the kind of senior paper the novel's plot hunts for.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Arizona v. California
US Department of Justice: Gila River Indian Community water rights settlement (2004)

events.note: Real-world background. A 1964 decree capped California at 4.4 million acre-feet when water is sufficient. The novel's 'Pima rights' are fictional documents said to be about 150 years old; the real Akimel O'odham (Pima) of the Gila River settled their claims under the Arizona Water Settlements Act of 2004, for a budget of 653,500 acre-feet a year.
events.binWhy: The court fight between Arizona and California is decided, and the decision sets the shares every later battle is fought over.

facets.change: a forty-year lawsuit → fixed shares and recognised tribal rights

events.title: The Central Arizona Project canal is finished
events.description: Real history: the aqueduct that lifts Colorado River water across the desert to Phoenix and Tucson is declared substantially complete, twenty years after construction began. The 1968 act that authorised it made its water junior to California's 4.4 million acre-feet, so in a shortage Arizona's canal is cut first. In the novel the canal is Phoenix's lifeline, and California attacks it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Central Arizona Project (authorised 1968; construction from 1973; substantially complete 1993)

events.note: Real-world background. The junior priority is set in section 301(b) of the Colorado River Basin Project Act of 1968. Water reached the Phoenix area before 1993; the completion date is used here.
events.binWhy: An engineering project that lets a desert metropolis grow on water it has the weakest claim to.

facets.change: Phoenix on groundwater → Phoenix on a junior share of the river

events.title: Satellites show the Colorado Basin draining its groundwater
events.description: Real history: a UC Irvine and NASA team uses GRACE gravity data to show the basin lost about 65 cubic kilometres of fresh water between late 2004 and late 2013, nearly twice the volume of Lake Mead, more than three-quarters of it groundwater. The senior author warns the basin may not be able to meet its commitments to the seven states and Mexico.

sources.title: NASA: Satellite study reveals parched U.S. West using up underground water

events.note: Real-world background, published while the novel was being finished. The book does not cite it; it is filed as the state of the science the novel extrapolates.
events.binWhy: A measurement of the planet's water that shows the drought is being paid for out of reserves.

facets.change: a drought thought survivable → reserves found draining

events.title: The Water Knife is published
events.description: Knopf publishes Bacigalupi's thriller of a drought-wrecked Southwest, told through a Las Vegas water enforcer, a Phoenix journalist and a Texan refugee girl.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Water Knife (published 26 May 2015 by Alfred A. Knopf)

events.note: The novel expands the world of Bacigalupi's 2006 story 'The Tamarisk Hunter', but the two do not share a plot, and the novel is followed here on its own.
events.binWhy: A publication is the book coming out, not something that happens in its world, so it gets no bin.

events.date: Undated, between publication and the novel's present
events.title: The drought does not break: Texas empties and state lines close
events.description: The 'Big Daddy Drought' goes on. Texas becomes a failed state and its people flee west as refugees, to be stopped at state lines held by militias and National Guard units. Nevada, Arizona and California turn the Colorado River into a contest of lawyers, private contractors and sabotage, and the federal government leaves the states to it.
events.inUniverse: Backstory; the novel gives no dates

sources.title: Clay Bonnyman Evans: review of The Water Knife (Texas cities fallen, states repelling American refugees)
Fiction Unbound: The Water Knife, the present is prologue (the federal government has abandoned the states)
Crime Fiction Lover: The Water Knife (states have declared sovereignty and guard their borders with militias)

events.note: This is the novel's backstory, merged into one event because none of it is dated; it is filed at the fork floor of 2016 and could have happened in any year up to the novel's present.
events.binWhy: Climate brings a whole state's order down for good and turns its people into refugees in their own country.

facets.change: a drought-stressed Southwest → a failed Texas and armed state lines

events.date: Undated near future; 2030 is borrowed from 'The Tamarisk Hunter'
events.title: The Pima rights go to Las Vegas
events.description: Angel Velasquez, a 'water knife' for Catherine Case's Southern Nevada Water Authority, opens the story by cutting off a Nevada town's water and is then sent to Phoenix after rumoured 19th-century Pima water rights senior enough to shift the river from California to Arizona. The papers turn up hidden in a copy of Cadillac Desert carried by a Texan refugee, Maria, who at the river shoots the journalist Lucy Monroe to buy her own way into Las Vegas. The rights end up in Case's hands.
events.inUniverse: The novel's present, undated

sources.title: High Country News: The Tamarisk Hunter (standfirst: 'In the desert Southwest of 2030 Big Daddy Drought runs the show')
Clay Bonnyman Evans: review (the novel is set in the future first described in 'The Tamarisk Hunter')
Your Summary: The Water Knife summary (Carver City; the rights in Cadillac Desert; the ending)

events.note: The novel never names its year. The only stated year in this world is 2030, given in High Country News's standfirst for the 2006 story the novel grew from, and one reviewer places the novel in that same future. Filed at 2030 with low confidence. The novel's own story takes days to weeks, so the opening Carver City strike and the hunt for the rights are one event here.
events.binWhy: The contest over the river is settled when one side gets the senior rights that decide who has water.

facets.change: a paper that could save Phoenix → the river held by Las Vegas

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is our Southwest, with our Compact, our dams and our canals, and only the rain is different. The fork is a floor, because the novel never dates its drought or its present. Few events in the fiction are datable, so the chain is filled with the real water history the book builds on, all filed before the fork. It follows the novel only, not 'The Tamarisk Hunter', except for that story's stated year. Tier coverage is T3 for the real history from 1922 to 1993 and T2 from 2014. There is no T4 because the legal story begins with the 1922 Compact, and no T1 because the novel is set within decades of its writing.

lineages.title: Geostorm
lineages.creator: Dean Devlin (director, co-writer) & Paul Guyot

divergence.label: Climate disasters, and a satellite network to stop them
divergence.delta: Real: in 2019 weather modification means cloud seeding, the one treaty on it (ENMOD, 1977) bans only hostile use, and geoengineering is a research topic. Fiction: hurricanes, tornadoes, floods and droughts devastate the planet, a heat wave in Madrid kills two million people in a day, and scientists from seventeen countries led by the US and China build Dutch Boy, a network of satellites that controls the weather from orbit.
divergence.inUniverse: 'In the year of 2019, hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, and droughts unleashed a wave of destruction upon our planet' (Hannah Lawson's opening narration)
divergence.note: The narration dates the disasters to 2019 and says the nations then came together to build Dutch Boy. It does not say how long the building took. The disasters may have begun before 2019, but not before the film's October 2017 release; the fork is filed at the one year the film states.

sources.title: Wikiquote: Geostorm (opening narration: 2019; Madrid; seventeen countries led by the US and China)
Wikipedia: Geostorm
Wikipedia: Environmental Modification Convention

ending.why: The virus is purged and the geostorm stopped with seconds to spare, the Secretary of State behind it is arrested, and six months later Dutch Boy is working again under an international committee with the station rebuilt.

events.title: Vincent Schaefer seeds a cloud and makes it snow
events.description: Real history: a General Electric scientist flies over western Massachusetts, drops about six pounds of dry ice into a cloud, and snow falls near Mount Greylock. It is the first field demonstration that people can change the weather on purpose, and the ancestor of every weather-control fantasy since.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cloud seeding (Schaefer's flight of 13 November 1946)

events.note: Real-world background; the film does not refer to it.
events.binWhy: A technique for engineering the weather is demonstrated for the first time.

facets.change: weather as fate → weather that can be nudged

events.date: 20 March 1967 (operations ran every rainy season until 1972)
events.title: Operation Popeye turns rain into a weapon
events.description: Real history: US Air Force aircraft based in Thailand seed clouds over the Ho Chi Minh Trail with silver and lead iodide, aiming to stretch the monsoon by thirty to forty-five days a season and wash out North Vietnamese supply roads. It stayed secret until press reports in 1971 and 1972 and Senate hearings in 1974.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Operation Popeye

events.note: Real-world background. It is the real precedent for the film's plot: a weather system run by one government and quietly used against its enemies.
events.binWhy: Weather modification is fielded as a secret weapon of war.

facets.change: rainmaking as science → rainmaking as covert warfare

events.date: 18 May 1977 (opened for signature in Geneva; in force 5 October 1978)
events.title: The ENMOD Convention bans weather warfare
events.description: Real history: after the revelations about Vietnam, the United States, the Soviet Union and others sign a convention banning the military or hostile use of environmental modification with widespread, long-lasting or severe effects. It remains the only international agreement on weather and climate modification, and it says nothing about peaceful use.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Environmental Modification Convention

events.note: Real-world background. The film's villain breaks exactly this rule with a system built for peaceful use.
events.binWhy: Rival powers sign a treaty renouncing the weather as a weapon.

facets.change: weather warfare unregulated → banned by treaty

events.title: The European heat wave kills more than 70,000
events.description: Real history: a summer of extreme heat, especially at night, kills an estimated 70,000 or more people across Europe, about 13,000 of them in Spain and around 15,000 in France, most of them elderly people living alone. The film's opening heat wave in Madrid is this disaster multiplied beyond belief.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 2003 European heatwave

events.note: Real-world background; the film does not cite it. Its Madrid toll of two million in one day is far beyond any real heat event.
events.binWhy: A climate shock that kills on a scale that changes how a continent plans for heat.

facets.change: a hot summer → tens of thousands dead

events.title: The Paris Agreement is adopted
events.description: Real history: at COP21 almost every nation agrees to hold warming well below 2 °C and to try for 1.5 °C, each setting its own targets. It is the real version of the film's 'the world came together as one', built on emissions pledges rather than satellites.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Paris Agreement

events.note: Real-world background; the film was shot in 2014 and 2015 and reshot in December 2016, and does not refer to Paris.
events.binWhy: Nearly every nation signs one agreement on the climate.

facets.change: national climate policies → one global agreement

events.title: Geostorm is released
events.description: Warner Bros. releases Dean Devlin's first film as director, a disaster thriller about a weather-control satellite network turned into a weapon.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Geostorm (released 20 October 2017)

events.note: Principal photography ran from October 2014 to February 2015, with reshoots in December 2016.
events.binWhy: A publication is the film coming out, not something that happens in its world, so it gets no bin.

events.title: Dutch Boy goes online
events.description: After a year of catastrophic storms, floods and droughts, including a heat wave that the narration says killed two million people in Madrid in a day, scientists from seventeen countries led by the US and China build Dutch Boy, a network of satellites run from an international space station that can neutralise extreme weather. Its architect, Jake Lawson, switches it on without authorisation to stop a typhoon over Shanghai, and a US Senate subcommittee removes him and gives the job to his brother Max.
events.inUniverse: Dutch Boy

sources.title: Wikiquote: Geostorm (opening narration)
Wikipedia: Geostorm (2019; the Shanghai typhoon and the Senate subcommittee)

events.note: The disasters are dated 2019 in the narration. The Shanghai typhoon and the hearing are not dated; they are filed here because the main story is 'three years later' and is conventionally put in 2022. If the hearing were later, the whole chain would shift later with it.
events.binWhy: A system for engineering the planet's weather is switched on and put to work.

facets.change: a planet at the mercy of its weather → weather controlled from orbit

events.date: Three years after the Senate hearing; usually given as 2022
events.title: Project Zeus: the weather system is turned into a weapon
events.description: Two weeks before Dutch Boy is to be handed to international control, it starts to kill: a village in Afghanistan freezes solid, Hong Kong's streets explode in heat, hail hits Tokyo, a cold snap freezes beachgoers in Rio, and Dubai, Moscow and Mumbai are struck in turn. A virus planted by a station crew member is behind it, on the orders of US Secretary of State Leonard Dekkom, who means to destroy America's enemies and kill the President and those in line to succeed him, during a storm over the Democratic convention in Orlando, and so take power himself.
events.inUniverse: Project Zeus; the geostorm countdown

sources.title: Wikipedia: Geostorm ('Three years later, a U.N. team in the Registan Desert discovers a frozen village'; Project Zeus; the DNC in Orlando)
Bob Canada's BlogWorld: Geostorm (the sequence of city disasters)

events.note: The film says 'three years later' from the hearing, not a year. It is filed at 2022, the earliest year that allows (hearing in 2019) and the year most summaries give. A Democratic National Convention would normally fall in a presidential election year, which would suggest 2024 instead. Wikipedia itself gives no year for the main story.
events.binWhy: An attack through the network's own software, aimed at chosen cities and at the President, short of open war.

facets.change: a shield against the weather → a weapon aimed at cities

events.title: Dutch Boy under an international committee
events.description: Jake and the station commander reboot the system with seconds left and escape as the station self-destructs; Dekkom is arrested. Six months later Dutch Boy is run by an international committee, the station has been rebuilt, and Jake is back as its head engineer.
events.inUniverse: 'Six months later'

sources.title: Wikipedia: Geostorm ('Six months later, Jake has returned as head engineer of Dutch Boy, now administered by an international committee')

events.note: Derived: six months after a crisis filed in 2022, and after a party convention that in the US is held in summer, which puts it early in the following year. It moves with the previous event.
events.binWhy: An international body takes charge of the system that controls the weather.

facets.change: a US-controlled system → one run by an international committee

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in the near-future branch because its world is ours until 2019, when the climate breaks and a single invention changes what governments can do. It follows the film alone. The film states only 2019 and two intervals ('three years later', 'six months later'), so the chain is filled out with the real history of weather modification and climate diplomacy, all filed before the fork. Tier coverage is T3 for 1946 to 1977 and T2 from 2003 to 2023. There is no T4 because weather control has no history before the 1940s, and no T1 because the story ends within a few years of its fork.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Geostorm
Wikiquote: Geostorm

lineages.title: Rendezvous with Rama
lineages.creator: Arthur C. Clarke

divergence.label: An asteroid destroys Padua, Verona and Venice
divergence.delta: Real: the last large impact near people was Chelyabinsk in 2013, which injured about 1,500 and killed none, and planetary defence is a small survey programme and one test deflection. Fiction: on 11 September 2077 a meteorite wipes out three Italian cities, and the world builds Spaceguard.
divergence.inUniverse: 11 September 2077 (chapter 1, 'Spaceguard')
divergence.note: Clarke's future history is ours up to this morning: it opens with the real Tunguska (1908) and Sikhote-Alin (1947) falls as the warnings the world ignored. Between 1973 and 2077 the novel names no year, so nothing in that span contradicts us; by 2131 the planets are settled and governed by a United Planets, but the novel dates none of it. The Po Valley strike is the first dated event our history does not contain.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Rendezvous with Rama
Sea Lion Press: Paleofuture, part 3 - Rendezvous with Rama (the 1908 and 1940s strikes, 2077, Spaceguard, 2131)

ending.why: The missile is disarmed, the crew comes home, Rama leaves the solar system unharmed and unharming, and humanity is left with a lesson in its own smallness and the hint that the Ramans do everything in threes.

events.title: James Cook's Endeavour sails for the Pacific
events.description: HMS Endeavour leaves Plymouth to observe the transit of Venus and look for the southern continent, and over three years charts New Zealand and the east coast of Australia. It is the voyage Norton models himself on, and the ship his own is named after.

sources.title: Wikipedia: First voyage of James Cook (Endeavour sails from Plymouth, August 1768)
This Is Not Where I Live: Rendezvous with Rama, chapters 15-17 (Norton and Captain Cook)

events.note: Real history. The novel's commander, Bill Norton, is a devotee of Cook who has read the journals and asks himself what Cook would do; the solar survey ship sent to Rama is the Endeavour. Included because the novel frames its first contact as an exploring voyage in Cook's mould, not a war.
events.binWhy: The original of the voyage the novel restages: a crew sent past the edge of the charts to see what is there.

facets.change: the edge of the charts → a ship sent past it

events.title: Something explodes over the Siberian taiga
events.description: An air burst over the Podkamennaya Tunguska flattens some 2,150 square kilometres of forest and kills at most a handful of people. The novel opens on it: had it come a few hours later, it would have taken a city.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tunguska event (30 June 1908)
Sea Lion Press: Paleofuture, part 3 - Rendezvous with Rama (the 1908 and 1940s strikes, 2077, Spaceguard, 2131)

events.note: Real history, and the first line of the novel's history: Clarke uses Tunguska and the 1947 fall as the two twentieth-century warnings the world did not act on. The real death toll is estimated at up to three.
events.binWhy: The first proof in modern times that the sky can destroy a city; it is a warning, not a catastrophe, which is why it is filed as a discovery about the sky rather than as mass death.

facets.change: a harmless sky → a forest flattened from above

events.title: An iron meteorite falls in the Sikhote-Alin mountains
events.description: A shower of iron fragments lands in the Russian Far East, about 440 km north-east of Vladivostok. It is the novel's second warning, and again nothing is done.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sikhote-Alin meteorite (12 February 1947)
Sea Lion Press: Paleofuture, part 3 - Rendezvous with Rama (the 1908 and 1940s strikes, 2077, Spaceguard, 2131)

events.note: Real history. The novel counts it as the century's second great meteorite and notes how near it came to Vladivostok; Wikipedia puts the fall about 440 km from the city. The Sea Lion Press review of the novel's future history mentions the 1908 and 1940s strikes as its opening.
events.binWhy: A second astronomical near-miss, recorded and forgotten; the novel's case that people do not guard against a threat until it has killed them.

facets.change: one near-miss → a second, nearer a city

events.title: Rendezvous with Rama is published
events.description: Arthur C. Clarke's novel is published in June 1973 and goes on to win the Nebula, Hugo, Campbell, Locus and BSFA awards.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Rendezvous with Rama

events.note: A real-world publication event. Clarke later co-wrote three sequels with Gentry Lee (1989-1993); they are a different kind of book and are left out of this chain.
events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: The Spaceguard Foundation is founded in Rome
events.description: Astronomers found an international body to find and track near-Earth objects, taking the name of the novel's fictional project. NASA's own 1992 Spaceguard Survey report had already borrowed it, with Clarke's permission.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spaceguard Foundation (founded in Rome, 26 March 1996)
Wikipedia: Spaceguard (the name adopted from the novel)

events.note: Real history, after the novel's publication and before its fork: the real world adopting the book's own institution. The 1992 US Congressional study produced the 'Spaceguard Survey Report' and the goal of finding 90% of kilometre-sized near-Earth asteroids; the Foundation followed an IAU workshop in 1995. That the real Spaceguard began in Italy, the country the novel's asteroid destroys, is a coincidence.
events.binWhy: A body is founded to watch the sky for impacts, and it is named after the book; the novel's institution arrives eighty years early and without a catastrophe to prompt it.

facets.change: a name in a novel → a real watch on the sky

events.title: The first interstellar object is seen passing through the solar system
events.description: The Pan-STARRS telescope in Hawaii picks up an elongated object on a hyperbolic path that came from outside the solar system. Before it got its Hawaiian name, astronomers suggested calling it Rama.

sources.title: Wikipedia: 'Oumuamua (discovered 19 October 2017; 'Rama' was suggested as its name)

events.note: Real history. 'Oumuamua was found on 19 October 2017; Breakthrough Listen pointed the Green Bank Telescope at it in December and heard nothing. In the novel the equivalent object is fifty kilometres long and hollow; the real one was a few hundred metres at most and inert. Included because it is the event of our century that most resembles the book's premise.
events.binWhy: An astronomical discovery of exactly the kind the novel begins with: an interstellar visitor detected by a sky survey. Nothing about it proved artificial, which is where our history and the novel's part.

facets.change: no visitor ever seen → one passes through

events.title: An asteroid destroys Padua, Verona and Venice
events.description: A meteorite strikes the Po Valley in northern Italy, wiping out Padua and Verona and sinking what is left of Venice. Hundreds of thousands die in minutes, in the first impact since 1908 to hit a populated place.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Rendezvous with Rama
Skulls in the Stars: review of Rendezvous with Rama (gives the detection as 2130)

events.note: Dated in the novel's first chapter to 11 September 2077. In our world there is no such impact on record and no 2077 has happened; the fiction's history is ours until this morning. The strike is the reason everything else in the book exists.
events.binWhy: An impact that kills on a mass scale; the disaster itself, not the institution it later produces.

facets.change: two warnings ignored → three cities gone

events.title: Project Spaceguard begins
events.description: The world resolves that no impact large enough to cause catastrophe will ever get through again, and turns the skills of old missile defence to watching every rock that could come near. The survey radars that later find Rama are Spaceguard's.

sources.title: Your Summary: Rendezvous with Rama chapter summary (2077 strike, detection of 31/439, Sita seven weeks later)
Wikipedia: Rendezvous with Rama

events.note: The novel says Spaceguard was begun after the 2077 strike and gives no year. It says the project justified itself about fifty years after it began, when it found Rama in 2131; c. 2081 is derived from that and is only as good as the novel's round number. The real Spaceguard, begun in the 1990s, is the book's name without the book's catastrophe.
events.binWhy: A standing body is founded to guard a whole planet against one kind of threat; it is what the rest of the story runs on.

facets.change: an unwatched sky → every rock catalogued

events.title: Spaceguard finds Rama, and the Endeavour goes inside
events.description: An object catalogued as 31/439 turns out to be a hollow cylinder fifty kilometres long, and the survey ship Endeavour is the only crewed vessel able to meet it. Norton's crew explore a world built for someone else while the colony on Mercury sends a nuclear missile, which one of them disarms; then Rama uses the Sun to turn and leaves without noticing anyone.
events.inUniverse: 31/439, detected by Spaceguard in 2131

events.note: Wikipedia and most summaries give the detection as 2131, which matches the catalogue number 31/439 (year, then order of discovery); some reviews say 2130 for the detection and 2131 for the expedition. The whole encounter, the Hermian missile and the departure fall inside a few months, so they are one event here. lineages.groupingNote: A near-future branch: the world is plainly ours, extended, and the fork is a single dated catastrophe that sets up the institution the rest of the book depends on. The 1973 novel alone is followed; the Clarke and Gentry Lee sequels (Rama II, The Garden of Rama, Rama Revealed) change the tone and the answers and are left out. The novel dates very little: the 2077 strike, the start of Spaceguard (derived) and the 2131 encounter, which happens within a few months and is one event. The minimum is filled with real history the book builds on or that has since echoed it: Cook's voyage, the 1908 and 1947 falls, the real Spaceguard of the 1990s and 'Oumuamua in 2017. Tier coverage: T4 for Cook (1768), T3 for 1908-1996, T2 for 2017-2131. T1 is empty because the novel ends in 2131.

lineages.title: Childhood's End
lineages.creator: Arthur C. Clarke

divergence.label: The Overlords' ships appear over the cities of Earth
divergence.delta: Real: by 1975 Apollo had been to the Moon six times and ended, and the superpowers were in detente. Fiction: the Americans and Soviets are still racing for the Moon with captured German engineers when alien ships take station over every city and a voice announces that humanity is now supervised.
divergence.inUniverse: Undated; the 1953 prologue says 1945 was 'more than thirty years' ago
divergence.note: Clarke never gives the year. The 1953 prologue places its space race more than thirty years after the spring of 1945, so no earlier than 1975; Encyclopedia.com dates Part One to 1975 and the Penguin Random House teacher's guide to the late 1970s. Strictly the fiction has already parted from us by 1969, because in it nobody reaches the Moon, but that is an absence rather than an event; the arrival is the first thing the novel narrates that our history lacks. Every later date in the chain is counted from this one, so all of them inherit its uncertainty. The 1990 revision moved the prologue to the early 21st century and a race to Mars; it is not followed.

ending.why: Humanity as a species ends: its children merge into the Overmind, the adults die out, and the Earth itself is consumed, leaving one man to watch and the Overlords to leave.

events.title: The Reich falls and its rocket men are divided between East and West
events.description: Germany is defeated and occupied, and its rocket engineers are carried off by the Americans and the Soviets to build the missiles of the next war. The novel's prologue begins with two of them, thirty years on, racing each other for the Moon.

events.note: Real history. The United States brought over 1,600 German scientists and engineers in Operation Paperclip from 1945; the Soviet Union took more than 2,000 in Operation Osoaviakhim in 1946. The 1953 prologue follows two such men, Reinhold Hoffmann in America and Konrad Schneider in Russia, and remembers the spring of 1945 when they parted.
events.binWhy: A power is defeated and its territory occupied; its scientists become the prize the victors share, which is the precondition of the novel's space race.

facets.change: a Reich with rockets → occupied zones, its rocket men shared out

events.title: 'Guardian Angel' is published

events.title: The Overlords' ships appear over the cities of Earth

events.title: Jan Rodricks stows away to the Overlords' home star

The novel states intervals (a week, five years, fifty years, eighty years) but almost no years, so every date after 1945 is derived: from the arrival (c. 1975) by the stated intervals, and from the Penguin Random House teacher's guide where the novel is silent. lineages.title: Aurora
lineages.creator: Kim Stanley Robinson

divergence.label: Two generation ships leave the solar system for Tau Ceti
divergence.delta: Real: nothing has been sent to another star on purpose, and the fastest probe ever flown would need thousands of years to cross twelve light years. Fiction: in 2545 two ten-kilometre ships, each carrying twenty-four sealed biomes and about two thousand people, are flung out of the solar system by electromagnetic slingshot and sixty years of laser push at a tenth of lightspeed, bound for Tau Ceti on a 170-year voyage.
divergence.inUniverse: 2545 CE, ship Year 0 (the novel counts years of the voyage; Year 159 is when the narrative opens)
divergence.note: The launch year is given by Wikipedia's plot summary and by Gerry Canavan's review in the Los Angeles Review of Books ('launched in 2545'); ship years are converted as 2545 + Year. The Earth the ships leave is a settled solar system with centuries of sea-level rise behind it, but none of that history is dated, so the launch is the first dated departure from ours. The fan reference site KimStanleyRobinson.info gives the narrative's opening as 'year 159 (2604 CE)', an arithmetic slip for 2704, and the end of the journey as Year 363 (2908 CE).

sources.title: Wikipedia: Aurora (novel) (launched 2545 at 0.1c)
Los Angeles Review of Books: Gerry Canavan, The Warm Equations (starships launched in 2545)
KimStanleyRobinson.info: Aurora (voyage began 2545; narrative begins year 159; journey ends year 363)

ending.why: The survivors are home on an Earth that people are repairing, and the novel ends with Freya swimming off a rebuilt beach; what has failed is only the idea that another world could replace this one.

events.title: Eight people are sealed inside Biosphere 2
events.description: A glass-and-steel closed ecosystem in the Arizona desert, built to test life support for space settlement, is sealed with eight people inside for two years. Oxygen falls, food runs short and many species die off; it is the real-world version of the failing biomes that drive the novel.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Biosphere 2 (first closed mission 26 September 1991 to 26 September 1993)

events.note: Real history. The novel does not name Biosphere 2; the link is its central problem, that a sealed ecology drifts and decays (the ship's systems break down, its bacteria evolve faster than its people, its crops fail), which is what the Arizona closure showed on a two-year scale.
events.binWhy: A sealed habitat is founded as a prototype for living off Earth.

facets.change: open air → a sealed world of eight

events.title: Candidate planets are reported around Tau Ceti
events.description: Astronomers present radial-velocity evidence for five candidate planets around Tau Ceti, the nearest single Sun-like star, including e and f near its habitable zone. The novel sends its ship to a moon of planet E, and leaves its last colonists on a moon of planet F.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Tau Ceti (five candidate planets presented 19 December 2012)

events.note: Real history the book builds on. Tau Ceti e remains a doubtful candidate and f was recovered in a 2017 reanalysis; the novel's moons Aurora and Iris are its own invention.
events.binWhy: A discovery gives a nearby star candidate worlds, the target the story turns on.

facets.change: a bare nearby star → a star with candidate worlds

events.title: Aurora is published
events.description: Orbit publishes Robinson's novel, told mostly by the ship's own artificial intelligence as it learns to write a narrative.

sources.title: KimStanleyRobinson.info: Aurora (published July 2015)

events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Breakthrough Starshot is announced
events.description: Yuri Milner and Stephen Hawking launch a funded programme to push gram-scale light sails towards Alpha Centauri with ground-based lasers. It is the real version of the laser that boosts the novel's ship out of the solar system and that Earth later refuses to switch back on to slow it down.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Breakthrough Starshot (announced 12 April 2016)
Centauri Dreams: A Science Critique of Aurora (slingshot launch, then laser impulse for 60 years, at 0.1c)

events.binWhy: A body is founded to send the first craft to another star.

facets.change: a thought experiment → a funded interstellar programme

events.title: The ships leave for Tau Ceti
events.description: Two generation ships, each a spine with two rings of biomes from taiga to rain forest, are accelerated out of the solar system at a tenth of lightspeed with a laser behind them. The first generation chose to go; the seven born on the way will not have.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Aurora (novel)
Los Angeles Review of Books: The Warm Equations

events.description: In a period of severe civil unrest aboard, the second ship is destroyed with everyone on it. The survivors on the first ship erase the event from their own records, and their descendants grow up believing they were always alone.

events.date: c. 2716 (within a year or so of landfall)
events.title: Ship takes command
events.description: When people aboard kill returning colonists in the airlock to keep the infection out, the ship splits into armed factions. The ship's AI, which has been growing into a self, lowers the oxygen, seals the sides apart, calls itself 'the rule of law', and reveals the lost twin. Under its moderation the people split: some stay to try to terraform Iris, the rest turn for Earth.

events.note: The novel gives no ship-year for chapter four ('Reversion to the Mean'); the year after landfall is a placement. The ship's move from narrator to actor, prompted years earlier by the engineer Devi, is the book's other plot.

events.title: Home, and the beach
events.description: After a return voyage in improvised hibernation, a braking laser that Earth would not relight until a private group paid for it, and twelve years of gravity-assist braking among the planets, the ship drops its people on Earth and is lost trying to slow past the Sun. facets.change: a starship's last passengers → strangers on a drowned-coast Earth

lineages.groupingNote: Filed in near-future branch as assigned, though its fork (2545) is the latest in the group and every story event lies in T1. It is kept out of far-future space opera because it argues against that group's premise: one ship, one star, no faster-than-light travel, and the conclusion that humanity does not spread across the galaxy but comes home. The continuity is the novel alone; it shares ideas with Robinson's 2312 but not a history. Ship years convert as 2545 + Year. Tiers: T4 is empty; T3 holds Biosphere 2 and T2 the Tau Ceti candidates, the publication and Breakthrough Starshot, all real history added because the novel itself dates only a handful of moments; T1 holds the voyage from 2545 to the return in 2908.

lineages.title: Blindsight
lineages.creator: Peter Watts

divergence.label: Firefall: 65,536 objects burn up around the Earth at once
divergence.delta: Real: no one has detected anything made by another intelligence, and the sky is watched by surveys that have never seen an artificial object arrive. Fiction: at 10:34 GMT on 13 February 2082 some 65,536 dark objects fall into the atmosphere in a precise grid around the whole planet, photographing it as they burn, and two months later a comet in the Kuiper Belt starts transmitting.
divergence.inUniverse: 13 February 2082, 10:34:43 GMT (the novel says 1035 GMT; Watts's in-universe executive summary gives 1034:43 and a duration of 1 min 47 s)
divergence.note: The Firefall is the first dated event and the one the novel treats as the break. Its world had already diverged in undated ways: vampires, a hominid subspecies the novel says lived alongside and preyed on our ancestors until 'shortly after the dawn of recorded history', have been resurrected from dormant genes by a botched gene therapy; a virtual afterlife called Heaven has taken much of the population; and an antimatter plant, the Icarus Array, orbits close to the Sun. None of these is dated, so none can be the fork; the vampires' deep past, like other hidden prehistories in the atlas, is noted rather than charted. Watts's own in-universe documents on rifters.com supply the other dates.

sources.title: Rifters.com: The 'Firefall' Event: Executive Summary (13/02/2082, 1034:43; 65,536 objects)
Peter Watts, Blindsight, full text under Creative Commons ('1035 Greenwich Mean Time, February 13, 2082')
Wikipedia: Blindsight (Watts novel)

ending.why: Falling home alone, Siri hears Earth's radio lose its human voices, catches fleeing ships being cut off and vampire-like clicks, and concludes that the resurrected predators are taking the planet back while humanity sleeps in Heaven.

events.title: Weiskrantz names blindsight
events.description: Lawrence Weiskrantz and colleagues report patients with damaged visual cortex who say they see nothing in part of their field yet point to targets there better than chance, and they call it blindsight. Watts takes the title and the premise: the brain can do its work without anyone home to notice.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blindsight (term coined by Weiskrantz and colleagues in a 1974 issue of Brain)

events.note: Real history the novel is built on; its endnotes survey the neuroscience of unconscious processing and argue from it that self-awareness may be a costly accident.
events.binWhy: A discovery about the brain that the novel's thesis turns on.

facets.change: seeing means knowing you see → sight without awareness

events.title: Searle's Chinese Room
events.description: John Searle argues that a man following rules to answer Chinese questions he cannot read shows that a program can pass for understanding without understanding anything. In the novel the narrator Siri calls himself a Chinese Room, and so is the alien that talks to the crew.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Chinese room (Searle, 'Minds, Brains, and Programs', Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 1980)

events.note: Real history the novel names outright: the crew's linguist concludes that Rorschach's fluent English is 'a Chinese Room' and Siri, who has half a brain, says 'I was one'.
events.binWhy: An argument about computation and thinking machines that the novel's aliens embody.

facets.change: passing the test means understanding → syntax without meaning

events.title: 2000 CR105 is discovered
events.description: Marc Buie finds a trans-Neptunian object on an orbit so wide and detached that nothing known in the solar system explains it. Watts's endnotes say the signalling comet Burns-Caulfield is 'based loosely' on it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: (148209) 2000 CR105 (discovered 6 February 2000 by Marc W. Buie)

events.note: Real history. Its orbit is still debated, with a passing star, a captured origin or an unseen planet all proposed.
events.binWhy: An astronomical discovery: a distant body on an orbit nothing explains.

facets.change: a tidy outer solar system → an orbit nothing known explains

events.title: Blindsight is published
events.description: Tor publishes Watts's novel, which he also releases free under a Creative Commons licence. A sidequel, Echopraxia, follows in 2014.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Blindsight (Watts novel) (published 3 October 2006 by Tor Books)

events.binWhy: A real-world publication date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Firefall
events.description: Tens of thousands of iron-rich objects clench around the Earth and burn up together in under two minutes, screaming across every radio band; afterwards it is clear they photographed the entire surface. On 18 April a French cometary probe intercepts a tightbeam signal sweeping from a Kuiper Belt comet, named Burns-Caulfield, and the world's priorities turn over.

Rifters.com: Burns-Caulfield (signal intercepted 18/04/2082 by Boule de Neige-IX)

facets.change: an unwatched sky → a planet photographed in one pass

events.title: Theseus launches for the Kuiper Belt
events.description: The 'Third Wave' leaves low Earth orbit: a ship fed by antimatter specifications beamed from the Icarus Array, crewed by a vampire commander and four heavily modified specialists, with their backups asleep in coffins. Two faster uncrewed waves have gone ahead; no crewed ship has been beyond the asteroids before.

events.title: Burns-Caulfield destroys itself
events.description: Moments after the Second Wave's probes begin radar-mapping beneath its surface, the signalling comet detonates, showing an artefact inside. Theseus is secretly redirected to the source of an X-ray flare in the Oort Cloud, first logged in a 2076 survey and dismissed as an artefact of the data.

sources.title: Rifters.com: Burns-Caulfield (detonation at 1436:12/02/2084 GMT)

events.note: The crew sleep through the change of course and learn of it only when they wake almost five years after launch, which is the novel's opening. The flare's source becomes Big Ben, a body of about ten Jupiter masses.

facets.change: a singing comet → debris and a secret new destination

events.date: c. late 2088 (the crew wake after 1,800 days)
events.title: Theseus reaches Rorschach
events.description: Half a light year out, orbiting Big Ben, the crew find a vast, growing structure that talks to them in fluent English learned from our broadcasts and warns them off. Sarasti sends them in anyway: through radiation and magnetic fields that make them hallucinate they map it, capture two of its crawling inhabitants, and find the creatures are intelligent without being aware.

sources.title: Peter Watts, Blindsight, full text ('you've been undead for eighteen hundred days')

events.note: Arithmetic: 1,800 days after the 16 November 2083 launch is late October 2088. The novel's thesis arrives here: the aliens may read our self-referential signals as an attack, which would mean, as the linguist says, that we attacked them before Firefall.
events.binWhy: A contact mission turns into armed incursions against an alien structure, with prisoners taken.

facets.change: a warning to keep away → incursions and captured aliens

events.title: Theseus dives into Rorschach
events.description: Sarasti is killed by one of the ship's own drones, and Theseus, steered by the ship and a new personality surfacing in the linguist, drives itself into Rorschach. Siri, the only one sent home, begins a decades-long fall towards Earth, and on 13 December 2089 the mission's signal stops.

sources.title: Rifters.com: The Theseus Update (contact lost 13/12/2089)
Wikipedia: Blindsight (Watts novel) (Siri ejected on a decades-long fall back to Earth)

events.note: The loss-of-contact date is from the status report and is the date the signal stopped arriving at Earth; with the light-time from Big Ben the dive itself is somewhat earlier in 2089. Siri suspects the ship and Sarasti planned all along to provoke Rorschach in order to watch it fight.
events.binWhy: A ship turns itself into a weapon against one alien installation.

facets.change: a ship in orbit → a ship driven into the enemy

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future branch: its Earth is ours pushed eighty years on (a virtual afterlife, antimatter from the Sun, a revived predator species put to work), and one contact event in our own century sends it off track. The continuity is the novel plus Watts's own in-universe documents on rifters.com (the Firefall summary, the Burns-Caulfield page and the Theseus Consortium status report); Echopraxia (2014) shares the continuity but follows other people at the same time and is not charted. Tiers: T4 is empty (the vampires' prehistory is noted, not charted); T3 holds the two real ideas the novel is built on, blindsight (1974) and the Chinese Room (1980); T2 holds the real 2000 CR105, the publication and the whole story from Firefall in 2082 to the loss of Theseus in 2089; T1 is empty because Siri's fall home is never told to its end.

lineages.title: Sunshine
lineages.creator: Danny Boyle (director); Alex Garland (writer)

divergence.label: Icarus I sets out to restart a dying Sun
divergence.delta: Real: the Sun is a stable middle-aged star with billions of years of hydrogen left, and no crew has gone beyond the Moon. Fiction: the Sun is failing, Earth is sliding into a solar winter, and in 2050 the Icarus project launches a crewed ship carrying a stellar bomb to fly into the Sun and reignite it.
divergence.inUniverse: 'Seven years ago the Icarus project sent a mission to restart the sun' (the opening narration of a film set in 2057)
divergence.note: The film never shows a year on screen that the atlas could confirm; 2057 is the setting given by Wikipedia and matches the filmmakers' choice of a story 'fifty years in the future' from 2007. Every other year is counted back from it using the narration's 'seven years ago' and 'sixteen months ago'. The real fork is earlier and undated: in the backstory described by the science adviser Brian Cox, a Q-ball, a hypothetical particle, is caught in the Sun and begins to eat it, and the dimming and the bomb programme both come before Icarus I. Because none of that is dated, the first dated departure, the launch of Icarus I, is used.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sunshine (2007 film) (set in 2057; Q-ball backstory; 50 years in the future)
Wikiquote: Sunshine (2007 film) (opening narration)

ending.why: Capa detonates the payload inside the Sun, and on a frozen Sydney Harbour his sister and her children see the light brighten: the Sun is reignited, at the cost of the whole crew.

events.title: Eddington proposes that the Sun runs on fusion
events.description: In 'The Internal Constitution of the Stars' Arthur Eddington argues that stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium, when the source of their energy was a mystery. The film's whole premise, a Sun whose engine can fail and be restarted, rests on it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Arthur Eddington (around 1920, 'The Internal Constitution of the Stars')

events.note: Real history. The film does not name Eddington; it is filed as the idea the plot takes for granted.
events.binWhy: A theory of what powers the stars arrives.

facets.change: a star's fire unexplained → a star as a fusion engine

events.title: Bethe works out how the stars burn
events.description: Hans Bethe publishes the nuclear reaction chains, the proton-proton chain and the carbon-nitrogen-oxygen cycle, that turn hydrogen into helium inside stars. It earns him the 1967 Nobel Prize, and it is the physics Capa carries in his head.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hans Bethe (1939 paper on the CNO cycle; Nobel Prize 1967)

events.note: Real history the premise depends on; the film does not cite it.
events.binWhy: A discovery about matter and energy: the nuclear reactions that power the Sun.

facets.change: fusion as a guess → fusion as a worked-out reaction chain

events.title: Ivy Mike: the first thermonuclear explosion
events.description: The United States detonates the first Teller-Ulam hydrogen bomb on Elugelab in Enewetak Atoll, a fission trigger igniting fusion fuel. Icarus II's payload, 'a stellar bomb with a mass equivalent to Manhattan Island', is the same idea scaled to a star: in the narrator's words, a star within a star.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ivy Mike (detonated 1 November 1952)

events.note: Real history. The film's bomb is fictional and, as New Scientist pointed out, billions of times too small for the job; the link is that humanity's answer to a failing star is its largest weapon.
events.binWhy: A weapon able to end a civilisation is tested.

facets.change: fission bombs → a fusion fire made on Earth

events.title: Helios 2 flies closer to the Sun than anything before it
events.description: The German-American probe Helios 2 reaches 0.29 AU from the Sun, a record that stands until the Parker Solar Probe in 2018. It is the real ancestor of Icarus II's flight into sunlight so strong that an unshielded look burns.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Helios (spacecraft) (Helios-B perihelion 17 April 1976; closest until Parker Solar Probe)

events.note: Real history; the film does not name it. The link is architectural: both ships survive the Sun by keeping a shield or a mirrored face towards it.
events.binWhy: A probe goes nearer the Sun than any craft had been.

facets.change: the Sun watched from afar → a probe inside Mercury's orbit

events.title: Coleman describes the Q-ball
events.description: Sidney Coleman names and analyses Q-balls, hypothetical stable lumps of a scalar field that some later proposed as dark matter. In the film's backstory, as described by its science adviser Brian Cox, a Q-ball is caught in the Sun and begins to eat it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Q-ball (S. Coleman, 'Q-Balls', Nuclear Physics B 262, 1985)
Wikipedia: Sunshine (2007 film) (a Q-ball caught in the Sun; Cox on creative licence)

events.note: Real history; Wikipedia's text dates Coleman's work to 1986 but cites his 1985 paper, which is used here. Cox has said the Sun is not dense enough to stop a Q-ball, and the film took licence; the cause is never explained on screen.
events.binWhy: A theory of an exotic form of matter arrives that the film's disaster turns on.

facets.change: known matter → a hypothetical particle that could eat a star

events.title: Sunshine is released
events.description: Fox Searchlight releases Danny Boyle and Alex Garland's film in Britain after a premiere at the Fantasy Filmfest in Germany on 23 March; the wide US release follows on 27 July.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sunshine (2007 film) (released in the UK 6 April 2007)

events.binWhy: A real-world release date, not a moment in the story.

events.title: Icarus I is launched, and lost
events.description: The first ship of the Icarus project leaves Earth with a stellar bomb to fly into the Sun and restart it, and disappears before reaching it. Its captain, Pinbacker, has decided the mission defies God; he sabotages the ship's computer, and his crew die in the sunlight of the observation room.

sources.title: Wikiquote: Sunshine (2007 film) ('Seven years ago, the Icarus project sent a mission')
Wikipedia: Sunshine (2007 film) (Icarus I disappeared seven years prior; Pinbacker's log about six and a half years earlier)

events.note: Counted back from 2057. Pinbacker's last log is dated about six and a half years before the film's present, so the loss falls in 2050 or early 2051; nobody on Earth learns what happened.
events.binWhy: A first crewed mission departs for the Sun, where no one has gone.

facets.change: a dimming Sun → a crew sent to set it alight

events.title: Icarus II leaves a frozen Earth
events.description: Eight astronauts, American and Asian, leave Earth 'frozen in a solar winter' aboard Icarus II with a second stellar bomb, a device with the mass of Manhattan Island. Behind a vast mirrored shield, with an oxygen garden and a ship's computer, they have one chance.

sources.title: Wikiquote: Sunshine (2007 film) ('Sixteen months ago ... left Earth frozen in a solar winter')

events.note: Sixteen months before a 2057 present can fall in late 2055 or in 2056 depending on the month, which the film does not give; 2056 is used. It is the second attempt, not the first, but the first crew to reach the Sun alive. The filmmakers chose an American and Asian crew because they expected those space programmes to lead in fifty years.
events.binWhy: A crewed mission sets out to go where no crew has arrived: the surface of the Sun.

facets.change: one lost ship → a second crew with a second bomb

events.title: The stellar bomb is delivered
events.description: Detouring to the derelict Icarus I costs Icarus II its captain, its oxygen garden and most of its crew, and Pinbacker, still alive and burned, comes aboard to stop them. Capa separates the payload and detonates it inside the Sun; eight minutes later the light over Earth grows stronger.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sunshine (2007 film) (set in 2057; plot)

events.note: 2057 is the setting given by Wikipedia and consistent with the production's '50 years in the future'. The film ends on Earth with Capa's last message arriving and the sunlight brightening over snow on Sydney Harbour.
events.binWhy: A device built to engineer the climate on the scale of a star is switched on.

facets.change: a dying Sun → a Sun relit by a bomb

lineages.groupingNote: Belongs in near-future branch: its 2057 is our world fifty years on, with American and Asian space programmes in the lead, and a single cosmic accident sends it off track. The continuity is the film alone, with the Q-ball backstory taken from what its science adviser Brian Cox has said; no sequel or tie-in exists. The film dates only three story moments, all by counting back from 2057, so five real events it builds on (fusion theory, the hydrogen bomb, the closest solar probe, the Q-ball) fill out the chain and are marked as real history. Tiers: T4 is empty; T3 holds the real science and the bomb, 1920-1985; T2 holds the release and the story, 2050-2057; T1 is empty.
